# Discipline Equals Freedom: Procedure, Not the Device, Creates Trust

**What it is** — Weber's closing chain in Lab 1C, credited to Jocko Willink's "discipline equals freedom": **discipline gives you reliability, reliability gives you confidence, confidence gives you decisions you can defend** (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.4; Lab 1C transcript 00:05:35–00:05:54). The claim just before it: "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures. A procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (transcript 00:04:45–00:05:02). Weber returns to the same chain twice more in the course. In Webinar 3 he operationalizes it as three practices — document repeatable procedures, set strategic direction with explicit decision boundaries, and give staff regular direct feedback — on the stated argument that this reduces ambiguity and gives both leaders and staff more room for focused work (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–00:38). In Module 6B Part B he applies the same chain to interdisciplinary communication: "the better educated the staff are... the less translation is needed. That frees up time for decision-making, problem-solving, and adaptation in real time" (Module_6B_Part_B PDF p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is that undocumented procedures create ambiguity, and ambiguity is what forces re-explanation, second-guessing, and disputes after the fact ("we took two measurements... which one is right?" PDF p.4). Writing the procedure down once removes the need to re-litigate it under pressure. **When to apply** — Any point where Eric is deciding whether a documented SOP is worth the paperwork: onboarding a new staff member or intern, standardizing a force-plate or GPS procedure, or writing a credential-vault protocol. **Eric's baseline:** a secure credential-vault protocol is already named as needed but not yet implemented [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4], and the intern curriculum's stated design principle is to teach "the how" (hands-on technical training) alongside "the why" (conceptual education) [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1]. **Inference:** the how is the procedure that makes the why defensible later.

It also assumes the underlying test or measure is worth running at all — see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] for that prior question.

**Example** — Weber's own test: "if you started a job this week as a lead in a department, would you be able to walk in and say, this is how we're going to operate?" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:05:13–00:05:23). **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's own Playbook still documents a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord collection SOP, even though roster-wide NordBord testing for football was retired after January 2023 [method-baseline.md Tensions #8]. **Inference:** this is the failure mode Weber warns against here, a procedure that fell out of sync with a decision that had already been made.

14	# Decide the Means Before the Modality, and the Modality Before the Technology
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's ordering rule for any training, testing, or monitoring decision: first name the **means** (the physical quality or question you are trying to change or answer, e.g. improving reactive strength or assessing hamstring capacity, illustrative examples, not Weber's own words), then choose the **modality** (the drill, test, or method), and only then pick the **technology**. Weber twice credits means-versus-modality to someone else, not himself: he calls it "an old Russian coaching accent" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:53–00:02:00; an evident ASR mishearing, likely "concept" or similar) and, later in the same recording, "an old thing. It's not mine" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:09:37–00:09:41). The same modality can serve different means: a sprint dribble drill can teach frontside mechanics or teach vertical force application depending on the coach's intent (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:28–00:03:09). He restates the same ordering twice more across the course: in Webinar 1 Part II, the summary reports that staff should begin with the athlete question or problem and only then select a measurement tool, rather than starting from the equipment on hand (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 00:00–02:14); and in Lab 2C's written material, the operating principle is stated directly: "Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then choose the technology" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's rationale: when technology leads, "we have force plates, so we should jump" and "we have GPS, so we should report something" become the operating logic, which he calls technology-led practice that "creates noise" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). Weber's own stated point is that without this shared language, "if people don't get that context, they're going to struggle with your communication" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:52–00:03:57). **Inference:** naming the means first likely gives staff a shared reason for a drill or test, so a leader can ask "what's the mean, why are you doing it?" and get an answer staff and athletes can act on (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:42–00:04:32).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any time a new device, test, or drill is proposed because it is available rather than because a specific quality or question has been named first. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's current Applied Performance data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport or question, which Eric's own gap analysis already flags as a usability problem [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]. **Inference:** this principle gives that gap a specific fix order, name the question and quality per sport first, then map which existing technology already answers it, before adding anything new.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that the technology still has real limitations that shape what's possible ("the technology is going to have limitations, of course, but the technology may be able to be applied in different ways," Lab 1A transcript, 00:04:38–00:04:50); this is an ordering rule for decision-making, not a claim that tool constraints are irrelevant. It also does not resolve which quality matters most for a given sport or phase, only the sequence in which the question gets asked.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's CM2 athlete-stage map (see [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]]) is the means-first vocabulary he built to make this ordering usable day to day: staff say where an athlete sits (control, movement, capacity, maximum) before discussing which drill or device to use next.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]] — the shared-language framework this principle is meant to produce. 14	# Protocol Drift: A Test Can Keep Its Name While Everything Else Changes
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's term for a specific reliability failure mode: a test keeps the same name over time while its warm-up, positioning, verbal instructions, or acceptance rules quietly change, so results are no longer comparable across sessions or staff even though the label on the report looks consistent (Podcast 1 summary, 02:19–03:03 and 04:24–05:31). His fix is the same one from Lab 1C: standardize and document those details before comparing results across time or personnel (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]).
17	
18	**Why it works** — **Inference:** protocol drift is dangerous specifically because it is likely invisible in the data itself; a change in average or peak value looks like an athlete change unless someone knows the procedure changed underneath it. Weber's own stated companion point, per the lesson summary, is a statistical-interpretation one: know the tool's and the local process's reliability before calling any individual change meaningful, and distinguish measurement noise from a change that warrants action (Podcast 1 summary, 03:03–03:17, 05:31–06:48).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any time staff turnover occurs on a testing team, a vendor pushes a software update that changes default settings, or a test is handed from one tester to another without a written procedure to follow. **Eric's baseline:** the current CMJ family runs a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol on ForceDecks [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], which is the kind of documented procedure this principle argues protects comparability. **Eric's baseline:** Eric's own corpus also shows two protocol documents giving different cueing instructions for the same CMJ test, the Assessment Manual says "do not coach the strategy of jumping," while Force Plate Testing V3 gives specific verbal cues [method-baseline.md Tensions #5]. **Inference:** this is itself a live example of the kind of undocumented drift this principle warns against.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — This principle addresses procedural consistency, not whether the test itself is the right one to run. **Inference:** a perfectly standardized bad test is still a bad test (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]]). It also does not by itself tell you the size of the error band a given procedure produces — that requires the reliability statistics in [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]].
23	
24	**Example** — Weber places any single product or test within a wider system: he warns against treating one red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete, and against collecting a measure without a defined question behind it (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24, 08:45–09:19). **Inference:** both are symptoms of a department that has not documented what a given result is supposed to trigger.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit that catches undocumented procedure. [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — the companion discipline against reacting to a single result. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where "what triggers action" gets formally defined.

# Discipline Equals Freedom: Procedure, Not the Device, Creates Trust

**What it is** — Weber's closing chain in Lab 1C, credited to Jocko Willink's "discipline equals freedom": **discipline gives you reliability, reliability gives you confidence, confidence gives you decisions you can defend** (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.4; Lab 1C transcript 00:05:35–00:05:54). The claim just before it: "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures. A procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (transcript 00:04:45–00:05:02). Weber returns to the same chain twice more in the course. In Webinar 3 he operationalizes it as three practices — document repeatable procedures, set strategic direction with explicit decision boundaries, and give staff regular direct feedback — on the stated argument that this reduces ambiguity and gives both leaders and staff more room for focused work (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–00:38). In Module 6B Part B he applies the same chain to interdisciplinary communication: "the better educated the staff are... the less translation is needed. That frees up time for decision-making, problem-solving, and adaptation in real time" (Module_6B_Part_B PDF p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is that undocumented procedures create ambiguity, and ambiguity is what forces re-explanation, second-guessing, and disputes after the fact ("we took two measurements... which one is right?" PDF p.4). Writing the procedure down once removes the need to re-litigate it under pressure. Weber's Webinar 3 material makes the same "frees attention" claim explicitly: predictable communication and clear roles reduce the time a leader spends interpreting routine requests, freeing that attention for planning and harder problems (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 00:00–00:59, 02:52–05:05).

**When to apply** — Any point where Eric is deciding whether a documented SOP is worth the paperwork: onboarding a new staff member or intern, standardizing a force-plate or GPS procedure, or writing a credential-vault protocol. **Eric's baseline:** a secure credential-vault protocol is already named as needed but not yet implemented [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4], and the intern curriculum's stated design principle is to teach "the how" (hands-on technical training) alongside "the why" (conceptual education) [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1]. **Inference:** the how is the procedure that makes the why defensible later.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a claim about where trust in a decision comes from, not a claim that more documentation is always better; Weber gives no guidance on how much procedure is enough or when documentation itself becomes the bottleneck. It also assumes the underlying test or measure is worth running at all — see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] for that prior question.

**Example** — Weber's own test: "if you started a job this week as a lead in a department, would you be able to walk in and say, this is how we're going to operate?" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:05:13–00:05:23). **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's own Playbook still documents a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord collection SOP, even though roster-wide NordBord testing for football was retired after January 2023 [method-baseline.md Tensions #8]. **Inference:** this is the failure mode Weber warns against here, a procedure that fell out of sync with a decision that had already been made.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this principle closes out. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — a structure that depends on this same procedure-first discipline. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]] — the communication-specific application from Webinar 3.

# Decide the Means Before the Modality, and the Modality Before the Technology

**What it is** — Weber's ordering rule for any training, testing, or monitoring decision: first name the **means** (the physical quality or question you are trying to change or answer, e.g. improving reactive strength or assessing hamstring capacity, illustrative examples, not Weber's own words), then choose the **modality** (the drill, test, or method), and only then pick the **technology**. Weber twice credits means-versus-modality to someone else, not himself: he calls it "an old Russian coaching accent" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:53–00:02:00; an evident ASR mishearing, likely "concept" or similar) and, later in the same recording, "an old thing. It's not mine" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:09:37–00:09:41). The same modality can serve different means: a sprint dribble drill can teach frontside mechanics or teach vertical force application depending on the coach's intent (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:28–00:03:09). He restates the same ordering twice more across the course: in Webinar 1 Part II, the summary reports that staff should begin with the athlete question or problem and only then select a measurement tool, rather than starting from the equipment on hand (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 00:00–02:14); and in Lab 2C's written material, the operating principle is stated directly: "Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then choose the technology" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's rationale: when technology leads, "we have force plates, so we should jump" and "we have GPS, so we should report something" become the operating logic, which he calls technology-led practice that "creates noise" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). Weber's own stated point is that without this shared language, "if people don't get that context, they're going to struggle with your communication" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:52–00:03:57). **Inference:** naming the means first likely gives staff a shared reason for a drill or test, so a leader can ask "what's the mean, why are you doing it?" and get an answer staff and athletes can act on (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:42–00:04:32).

**When to apply** — Any time a new device, test, or drill is proposed because it is available rather than because a specific quality or question has been named first. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's current Applied Performance data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport or question, which Eric's own gap analysis already flags as a usability problem [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]. **Inference:** this principle gives that gap a specific fix order, name the question and quality per sport first, then map which existing technology already answers it, before adding anything new.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that the technology still has real limitations that shape what's possible ("the technology is going to have limitations, of course, but the technology may be able to be applied in different ways," Lab 1A transcript, 00:04:38–00:04:50); this is an ordering rule for decision-making, not a claim that tool constraints are irrelevant. It also does not resolve which quality matters most for a given sport or phase, only the sequence in which the question gets asked.

**Example** — Weber's CM2 athlete-stage map (see [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]]) is the means-first vocabulary he built to make this ordering usable day to day: staff say where an athlete sits (control, movement, capacity, maximum) before discussing which drill or device to use next.

**Related** — [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]] — the shared-language framework this principle is meant to produce. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the same purpose-first ordering applied specifically to monitoring vs. testing decisions. [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the companion discipline once a measurement is in hand.

# Protocol Drift: A Test Can Keep Its Name While Everything Else Changes

**What it is** — Weber's term for a specific reliability failure mode: a test keeps the same name over time while its warm-up, positioning, verbal instructions, or acceptance rules quietly change, so results are no longer comparable across sessions or staff even though the label on the report looks consistent (Podcast 1 summary, 02:19–03:03 and 04:24–05:31). His fix is the same one from Lab 1C: standardize and document those details before comparing results across time or personnel (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]).

**Why it works** — **Inference:** protocol drift is dangerous specifically because it is likely invisible in the data itself; a change in average or peak value looks like an athlete change unless someone knows the procedure changed underneath it. Weber's own stated companion point, per the lesson summary, is a statistical-interpretation one: know the tool's and the local process's reliability before calling any individual change meaningful, and distinguish measurement noise from a change that warrants action (Podcast 1 summary, 03:03–03:17, 05:31–06:48).

**When to apply** — Any time staff turnover occurs on a testing team, a vendor pushes a software update that changes default settings, or a test is handed from one tester to another without a written procedure to follow. **Eric's baseline:** the current CMJ family runs a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol on ForceDecks [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], which is the kind of documented procedure this principle argues protects comparability. **Eric's baseline:** Eric's own corpus also shows two protocol documents giving different cueing instructions for the same CMJ test, the Assessment Manual says "do not coach the strategy of jumping," while Force Plate Testing V3 gives specific verbal cues [method-baseline.md Tensions #5]. **Inference:** this is itself a live example of the kind of undocumented drift this principle warns against.

**When NOT to apply** — This principle addresses procedural consistency, not whether the test itself is the right one to run. **Inference:** a perfectly standardized bad test is still a bad test (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]]). It also does not by itself tell you the size of the error band a given procedure produces — that requires the reliability statistics in [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]].

**Example** — Weber places any single product or test within a wider system: he warns against treating one red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete, and against collecting a measure without a defined question behind it (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24, 08:45–09:19). **Inference:** both are symptoms of a department that has not documented what a given result is supposed to trigger.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit that catches undocumented procedure. [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — the companion discipline against reacting to a single result. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where "what triggers action" gets formally defined.

# Decision Gates: Five Elements That Turn Data Into a Decision

**What it is** — A decision gate is "a predefined checkpoint in your workflow where you review agreed criteria and make a clear call before progressing: Go / Modify / Stop" (Lab_2D_Decision_Gates.pdf p.1). Weber's five required elements: **(1) what's being evaluated** — named specifically enough to build criteria around (not "hamstring injury" but "eccentric knee flexor strength" or "sprint exposure tolerance, defined speed band and volume"); **(2) criteria** — pass (green, proceed), fail (red, stop/regress), and borderline (amber, confirm/repeat/add a data point), plus an explicit definition of what counts as a breach; **(3) decision options** — progress, hold, regress, refer, escalate, matched to the sport's and medical setup's actual resources; **(4) ownership** — who provides inputs, who interprets results, and who owns the final call, since "if ownership is unclear, gates become meetings instead of decisions"; **(5) next step** — the immediate action a pass, fail, or borderline result triggers, including a re-test or review timeframe (pp.1–2). Weber also insists gates carry logistics-realistic timeframes stated in advance ("First clinical review happens within X hours," "Imaging is expected within Y days if criteria are met") so a department is not improvising timelines after an injury occurs (p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated mechanism: when staff send raw reports to coaches and senior medical staff without a pre-agreed structure, "people interpret numbers differently, and emotion enters the room, especially around selection" (p.2). **Inference:** agreeing the five elements before the pressure of an actual decision arrives removes the negotiation from the moment it is least likely to go well.

**When to apply** — Any recurring return-to-play, load-progression, or technology-adoption decision that currently gets re-litigated case by case. **Eric's baseline:** "KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing" is named as a departmental operating principle, but "no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus" [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** this framework is a direct template for building that missing protocol, element by element.

**When NOT to apply** — A decision gate is indefensible without knowing how noisy the underlying measurement is; Weber's own next lab makes this explicit — see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the statistics a gate's criteria depend on. This framework also assumes a genuine, pre-identifiable decision point exists; it is not suited to open-ended diagnostic or brainstorming work (see [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] for when "decide" is the wrong mode to reach for).

**Example** — Weber's own lab task: build one performance gate (e.g., speed-exposure progression) and one rehab gate (e.g., hamstring return-to-run), each specifying key quality, pass/fail/borderline criteria, decision options, ownership, and next step plus timeframe (p.3).

**Related** — [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistical foundation a gate's criteria need. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — where the "if this result, then this action" decision matrix first appears. [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]] — the record-keeping companion to a gate's decision.

# Decision Gates: Five Elements That Turn Data Into a Decision

**What it is** — A decision gate is "a predefined checkpoint in your workflow where you review agreed criteria and make a clear call before progressing: Go / Modify / Stop" (Lab_2D_Decision_Gates.pdf p.1). Weber's five required elements: **(1) what's being evaluated** — named specifically enough to build criteria around (not "hamstring injury" but "eccentric knee flexor strength" or "sprint exposure tolerance, defined speed band and volume"); **(2) criteria** — pass (green, proceed), fail (red, stop/regress), and borderline (amber, confirm/repeat/add a data point), plus an explicit definition of what counts as a breach; **(3) decision options** — progress, hold, regress, refer, escalate, matched to the sport's and medical setup's actual resources; **(4) ownership** — who provides inputs, who interprets results, and who owns the final call, since "if ownership is unclear, gates become meetings instead of decisions"; **(5) next step** — the immediate action a pass, fail, or borderline result triggers, including a re-test or review timeframe (pp.1–2). Weber also insists gates carry logistics-realistic timeframes stated in advance ("First clinical review happens within X hours," "Imaging is expected within Y days if criteria are met") so a department is not improvising timelines after an injury occurs (p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated mechanism: when staff send raw reports to coaches and senior medical staff without a pre-agreed structure, "people interpret numbers differently, and emotion enters the room, especially around selection" (p.2). **Inference:** agreeing the five elements before the pressure of an actual decision arrives removes the negotiation from the moment it is least likely to go well.

**When to apply** — Any recurring return-to-play, load-progression, or technology-adoption decision that currently gets re-litigated case by case. **Eric's baseline:** "KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing" is named as a departmental operating principle, but "no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus" [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** this framework is a direct template for building that missing protocol, element by element.

**When NOT to apply** — A decision gate is indefensible without knowing how noisy the underlying measurement is; Weber's own next lab makes this explicit — see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the statistics a gate's criteria depend on. This framework also assumes a genuine, pre-identifiable decision point exists; it is not suited to open-ended diagnostic or brainstorming work (see [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] for when "decide" is the wrong mode to reach for).

**Example** — Weber's own lab task: build one performance gate (e.g., speed-exposure progression) and one rehab gate (e.g., hamstring return-to-run), each specifying key quality, pass/fail/borderline criteria, decision options, ownership, and next step plus timeframe (p.3).

**Related** — [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistical foundation a gate's criteria need. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — where the "if this result, then this action" decision matrix first appears. [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]] — the record-keeping companion to a gate's decision.

16	**What it is** — A two-part audit that extends Lab 1C's tech-stack inventory (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) from what a department has to what it produces and who acts on it. The **capability audit** is the "tool truth": what a technology measures, what it does not measure, and where its use shifts from measurement into inference (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1). The **workflow audit** covers who captures the data, how it is processed (vendor software, in-house code, dashboards), who interprets it, how it is communicated, and where the decision actually gets made (p.1). Built as a matrix: technologies down the rows, applications across the columns (either by domain — rehab, performance, return-to-play, monitoring — or by question — hamstring injury, speed development, deceleration ability, fatigue monitoring). Each cell gets four entries: purpose (what question it answers), output (the metric/report delivered), owner (who is responsible), and workflow (capture to process to interpret to communicate to decision) (pp.1–2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: "a device doesn't create impact. A workflow does" (p.1). In small environments alignment happens informally because people talk constantly; as staff, tools, and handoffs multiply, "alignment must be designed, not hoped for" (p.1). **Inference:** the matrix likely works by forcing that design decision into a written artifact rather than leaving it as tribal knowledge that breaks when a single staff member leaves. The same audit embeds a delegation model: Weber frames the department's direction and standards as "the highway" and staff's day-to-day tool and timing choices as "changing lanes," with the matrix giving staff **tactical freedom while maintaining strategic alignment** (p.1–2); see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] for the fuller treatment of that mental model.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Onboarding new staff, identifying budget or technology gaps, or auditing an existing department for handoff risk. **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and Athletic Medicine's decisions, a support/advisory role rather than a stated final-decision role [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play], and the baseline notes (Tension #2) that the Playbook's peer-department framing and a support-staff framing are not reconciled in the corpus. Inference: Weber's hamstring triangulation example (Lab_2b PDF p.2: force transducer strength trend, GPS/IMU exposure dose, mechanics check, immediate and 24 h response checks) is the kind of shared workflow this matrix would specify, with an owner named for each step.

25

14	# The Decision Pathway: Six Stages, Five Gaps to Audit
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's model of the full route from an observation to an action: **data capture -> quality control -> analysis -> interpretation -> communication -> decision and action** (Video Lab 6D summary, 00:00–02:02). He names a specific gap between each pair of adjacent stages. **(1) Dirty data** (capture to quality control): check that the collection protocol was actually followed and that anomalies are caught before entering reports or a long-term database, with a named owner for the check. **(2) Expertise** (quality control to analysis): a reliable measurement can still be judged against an unsuitable threshold, or without its normal context, including software defaults that were never reviewed. **(3) Interpretation** (analysis to meaning): a number can reach a meeting with no one stating what it means for the athlete or the decision, and excess data can exceed the team's capacity to interpret it. **(4) Communication** (interpretation to decision-maker): technical language can obscure the actual requested action; Weber recommends leading with a clear recommendation and supplying supporting detail in a form the recipient can use. **(5) Authority** (recommendation to action): even a clear recommendation can be ignored without a formal decision gate or override process; he calls for explicit decision authority and a record of recommendations and decisions (02:02–10:50).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: pathways break "not because the people are bad at jobs, but the process has a gap. Steps are not defined and people's roles within those steps are not defined" (6D transcript 00:00:42 to 00:00:52), and naming the stages lets a team "name exactly where your pathway is breaking" (00:00:57 to 00:01:06). Inference: this is the same diagnostic logic as [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]], applied to a single decision's pipeline.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Weber's own stated practical use: trace a recent important decision through all six stages, identify the gap that most affects decisions, and assign a concrete owner and process to close it (10:52–12:11). **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar) rather than by sport, with no sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently documented [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment; Load monitoring and GPS]. **Inference:** Weber's expertise-gap point, that someone needs to set and review the thresholds a measurement is judged against, including software defaults, lands directly on that named gap; this framework gives it a specific owner-and-process fix rather than leaving it as a general observation.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — This framework audits the pipeline's structure; it does not itself validate whether a given threshold or software default is the right one, only that someone should be reviewing it. It also assumes a decision pathway already exists to be traced — for a genuinely new signal with no established pathway, the encoding and integration frameworks (see [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]]) are the prior step.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's communication-gap framing: leading with a clear recommendation first, and putting supporting technical detail in a form the recipient can actually use, rather than requiring the recipient to extract the recommendation from technical language themselves (05:32–08:54) — the same discipline as [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] applied specifically at the decision-pathway's communication stage.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] — the department-level companion to this pipeline-level audit. [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — the communication-gap discipline this framework names as stage four. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the formal structure for stage five's authority and action.

13	
14	# Evidence Stacking: Don't Decide on One Dramatic Signal
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's central question for any consequential decision, per the lesson summary: does staff have enough independent, relevant information to act (Podcast 2 summary, 00:00–02:20). A dramatic single result or first impression should prompt further investigation, not settle the decision. An evidence stack combines the event/problem history, clinical findings where relevant, the athlete's own prior results, movement and capacity checks, and performance under the conditions the decision actually concerns (00:00–02:20). His practical takeaway: define the decision first, identify the important unanswered questions, then choose measures that each add distinct evidence rather than repeating what is already known (17:35–18:15). This is the same caution Weber repeats in narrower form elsewhere in the course: in Lab 2A, one test returning to baseline is treated as one data point rather than a stand-alone clearance (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02); in Webinar 1 Part III, one favorable test result is not a complete return-to-running answer (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 07:44–08:54); and in Podcast 1, he warns specifically against treating a single red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's own stated purpose, per the lesson summary, is to separate meaningful change from noise and to communicate decisions with appropriate confidence (Podcast 2 summary, 00:00–02:20). **Inference:** the likely reason combining sources helps is that different evidence types fail in different, largely independent ways: a single clinical impression, a single hop-test result, and a single speed-exposure metric can each individually mislead, but they are unlikely to all mislead in the same direction at once. Updating the working assessment as each new piece arrives, illustrated with Weber's soccer-knee and hamstring anecdotes (02:20–17:35), is more robust than treating any one piece as decisive.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any return-to-play, load, or selection decision where one metric alone is being used to justify the call, especially under time pressure or when a result is unusually dramatic (very good or very bad). **Eric's baseline:** the course transcripts in Eric's own corpus argue "you don't need a fancy test or anything to do that. But you do have to have a good coach's eye," while Eric's own SportSmith writing moved the opposite direction on daily monitoring by replacing subjective wellness surveys with objective mRSI [method-baseline.md Tensions #3]. **Inference:** evidence stacking offers a synthesis rather than forcing a choice between those two positions: the coach's eye is one more independent stream to stack alongside the objective metric, not a competitor to it.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Per the lesson summary's own caveat (not Weber's words), the anecdotes illustrate a reasoning approach and do not establish that a triple-hop baseline can diagnose a knee injury; medical diagnosis and clearance remain clinical decisions (Podcast 2 summary, practical takeaway). It also does not specify how many independent streams are enough for a given decision; that judgment is left to the practitioner.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's hamstring case: clinical progress and gym measures were supplemented with hopping, running-speed exposure, and a comparison of running mechanics at matched speeds, specifically to close the gap between controlled tests and actual field demands before returning the athlete to competition (Podcast 2 summary, 10:30–17:35). The reported outcome is one case, not a validated return-to-play rule. Untested anecdote (n=1). The mechanics comparison used SpeedSig, Weber's own product (Podcast 2 transcript 00:15:52 to 00:16:18); treat the case as an illustration by an interested party, not evidence for the product or the return pathway.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the single-measurement discipline this framework scales up. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where a completed evidence stack feeds a formal go/hold/stop decision. [[principle--protocol-drift-undermines-comparability]] — the reliability discipline each stream in the stack still needs individually.
27

13	
14	# The Integration Problem: Five Break Points Between Data and Decision
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's framework for a specific failure mode: a practitioner collects genuinely useful information, but it never influences a decision because the organization has no reliable way to interpret, discuss, or act on it. "Good information does not guarantee influence... this is usually not a knowledge problem" (The_Leader_s_Integration_Cheat_Sheet.pdf p.1). His five break points, tracing a signal from collection to action: **(1) language gap** — teams use different terms or underlying models for athlete status, readiness, risk, or rehabilitation; **(2) decision pathway gap** — no agreed route identifies who collects, reviews, discusses, and uses technical information, or what triggers a conversation; **(3) authority gradient** — a senior decision-maker can override a technical recommendation without discussion or explanation (Weber favors hearing competing cases and explaining the decision, rather than a silent override); **(4) relationship deficit** — the person who must act does not yet understand or trust the evidence; per the lesson summary, Weber frames this as a shared responsibility, with practitioners sharing responsibility for preparing colleagues to interpret new information; **(5) process absence** — missing meeting gates, decision checkpoints, or review steps let a team skip important intermediate judgments (Video Lab 6A summary, 06:58–13:14; cheat sheet p.1). His diagnostic test: "if your recommendation changes as it moves up the chain, there is likely an integration leak" (cheat sheet p.1).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's core claim, stated directly, is that departments fail through structure, not intent: recommendations get ignored, diluted, or misunderstood because the environment lacks the pathway to handle them, not because the underlying analysis was wrong (cheat sheet p.1). **Inference:** naming five distinct break points turns a vague sense that good work isn't landing into a specific, auditable question, which of the five links actually failed.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Reviewing a past decision where technically sound information did not change the outcome, or auditing a department's current pathway for a specific recurring signal (e.g., a fatigue flag, an asymmetry finding). Weber's own audit question directly names the exercise: "you need to ask whether your data has ever directly changed a major decision, and whether you can trace the path from collection to action" (cheat sheet p.1). **Eric's baseline:** KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing is named as a departmental operating principle, but no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in the reviewed corpus [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** Weber's audit question is a useful test to run against that specific gap.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own account of a past bone-stress-injury case, where he says he had not communicated his evidence in a form colleagues could use, is a personal anecdote illustrating the communication point; it does not establish a general injury-prediction rule from training surface, and the transcript cannot verify the causal claim (Video Lab 6A summary, 13:14–15:38). This framework also assumes the underlying information was sound in the first place; it diagnoses pathway failure, not measurement or inference failure (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] for that separate question).
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's authority-gradient distinction: overriding a technical recommendation, in the course's words, "sometimes that is necessary, but it should happen transparently and with explanation" (cheat sheet p.1) — the failure mode is the silent override, not the override itself.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]] — the next-stage problem (same information, different disciplinary lens) that this framework's language gap connects to. [[framework--decision-pathway-six-stages-five-gaps]] — a parallel, more granular breakdown of the data-to-decision pipeline. [[framework--grey-zone-overlap-ownership]] — where the authority gradient is resolved for medical/performance overlap specifically.
27

His five break points, tracing a signal from collection to action: **(1) language gap** — teams use different terms or underlying models for athlete status, readiness, risk, or rehabilitation; **(2) decision pathway gap** — no agreed route identifies who collects, reviews, discusses, and uses technical information, or what triggers a conversation; **(3) authority gradient** — a senior decision-maker can override a technical recommendation without discussion or explanation (Weber favors hearing competing cases and explaining the decision, rather than a silent override); **(4) relationship deficit** — the person who must act does not yet understand or trust the evidence; per the lesson summary, Weber frames this as a shared responsibility, with practitioners sharing responsibility for preparing colleagues to interpret new information; **(5) process absence** — missing meeting gates, decision checkpoints, or review steps let a team skip important intermediate judgments (Video Lab 6A summary, 06:58–13:14; cheat sheet p.1). His diagnostic test: "if your recommendation changes as it moves up the chain, there is likely an integration leak" (cheat sheet p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's core claim, stated directly, is that departments fail through structure, not intent: recommendations get ignored, diluted, or misunderstood because the environment lacks the pathway to handle them, not because the underlying analysis was wrong (cheat sheet p.1). **Inference:** naming five distinct break points turns a vague sense that good work isn't landing into a specific, auditable question, which of the five links actually failed.

**When to apply** — Reviewing a past decision where technically sound information did not change the outcome, or auditing a department's current pathway for a specific recurring signal (e.g., a fatigue flag, an asymmetry finding). Weber's own audit question directly names the exercise: "you need to ask whether your data has ever directly changed a major decision, and whether you can trace the path from collection to action" (cheat sheet p.1). **Eric's baseline:** KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing is named as a departmental operating principle, but no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in the reviewed corpus [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** Weber's audit question is a useful test to run against that specific gap.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own account of a past bone-stress-injury case, where he says he had not communicated his evidence in a form colleagues could use, is a personal anecdote illustrating the communication point; it does not establish a general injury-prediction rule from training surface, and the transcript cannot verify the causal claim (Video Lab 6A summary, 13:14–15:38). This framework also assumes the underlying information was sound in the first place; it diagnoses pathway failure, not measurement or inference failure (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] for that separate question).

**Example** — Weber's authority-gradient distinction: overriding a technical recommendation, in the course's words, "sometimes that is necessary, but it should happen transparently and with explanation" (cheat sheet p.1) — the failure mode is the silent override, not the override itself.

**Related** — [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]] — the next-stage problem (same information, different disciplinary lens) that this framework's language gap connects to. [[framework--decision-pathway-six-stages-five-gaps]] — a parallel, more granular breakdown of the data-to-decision pipeline. [[framework--grey-zone-overlap-ownership]] — where the authority gradient is resolved for medical/performance overlap specifically.

# The Capability and Workflow Audit Matrix

**What it is** — A two-part audit that extends Lab 1C's tech-stack inventory (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) from what a department has to what it produces and who acts on it. The **capability audit** is the "tool truth": what a technology measures, what it does not measure, and where its use shifts from measurement into inference (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1). The **workflow audit** covers who captures the data, how it is processed (vendor software, in-house code, dashboards), who interprets it, how it is communicated, and where the decision actually gets made (p.1). Built as a matrix: technologies down the rows, applications across the columns (either by domain — rehab, performance, return-to-play, monitoring — or by question — hamstring injury, speed development, deceleration ability, fatigue monitoring). Each cell gets four entries: purpose (what question it answers), output (the metric/report delivered), owner (who is responsible), and workflow (capture to process to interpret to communicate to decision) (pp.1–2).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: "a device doesn't create impact. A workflow does" (p.1). In small environments alignment happens informally because people talk constantly; as staff, tools, and handoffs multiply, "alignment must be designed, not hoped for" (p.1). **Inference:** the matrix likely works by forcing that design decision into a written artifact rather than leaving it as tribal knowledge that breaks when a single staff member leaves. The same audit embeds a delegation model: Weber frames the department's direction and standards as "the highway" and staff's day-to-day tool and timing choices as "changing lanes," with the matrix giving staff **tactical freedom while maintaining strategic alignment** (p.1–2); see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] for the fuller treatment of that mental model.

**When to apply** — Onboarding new staff, identifying budget or technology gaps, or auditing an existing department for handoff risk. **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and Athletic Medicine's decisions, a support/advisory role rather than a stated final-decision role [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play], and the baseline notes (Tension #2) that the Playbook's peer-department framing and a support-staff framing are not reconciled in the corpus. Inference: Weber's hamstring triangulation example (Lab_2b PDF p.2: force transducer strength trend, GPS/IMU exposure dose, mechanics check, immediate and 24 h response checks) is the kind of shared workflow this matrix would specify, with an owner named for each step.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a documentation and role-clarity exercise, not a validation of any individual test's reliability (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] and [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question). Weber's own hamstring/deceleration examples are illustrations of matrix structure, not a validated injury-assessment or programming pathway.

**Example** — Weber's deceleration-capacity workflow: GPS/IMU captures high-intensity deceleration events, data is processed (Python/R/SpeedSig), the output becomes a trend report plus exposure-tolerance summary, and the decision becomes a programming adjustment to load, density, or drill selection (p.3).

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the prior-step audit this one builds on. [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] — the delegation model embedded in this matrix. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where the "decision" cell of this matrix gets formalized.

# CM²: Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum

**What it is** — A four-stage shared map Weber uses to describe where an athlete sits in a program, so staff across strength and conditioning, rehab, and sports science can communicate quickly without re-litigating vocabulary. The stages: **Control** (single-joint, isolated activation, used early in rehab or with an athlete who cannot yet sequence joints), **Movement** (multi-joint, integrated patterns that are "viable and repeatable... without falling apart"), **Capacity** (building the "engine": volume and tolerance for work, where "a lot of athletes live for large parts of the year"), and **Maximum** (short exposures to peak speed, force, or power once capacity is built) (Lab 1A transcript, 00:06:05–00:08:32; Lab_1A_Blog_Building_a_Common_Language.pdf p.2, stage definitions). Athletes move forward when ready and back to an earlier stage when needed. The model is CM² (Lab_1A_Blog_Building_a_Common_Language.pdf p.1 and p.2: "CM² – Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum"). The transcript renders it "CM2" (00:06:10), "STM squared" (00:09:21) and "CM squared" (00:09:41), all ASR variants.

**Why it works** — Weber's stated rationale is coordination, not physiology: a large staff (athlete, performance manager, several S&C coaches, athletic trainers, physios, sports science staff) needs "this very, very simple language that can be utilized between multiple domains of practitioners easily to allow people to move quickly and not get bogged down" (00:08:42–00:08:55). Placing an athlete on the map ("he's not moving that well, we need to drop him back to control") gives a leader a one-line status update across disciplines without needing agreement on deeper theory.

**When to apply** — As a discussion shorthand in interdisciplinary handoffs (rehab to performance, performance to sport coach) when the question is where an athlete sits in the process rather than a specific numeric threshold. **Eric's baseline:** the Vermeil hierarchy (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass" [method-baseline.md, Strength and power]. **Inference:** CM2 maps loosely onto that same staged logic, so it could sit alongside rather than replace that existing shared vocabulary.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber presents this as one example teams can adapt, not a validated developmental model ("I made my [CM2] thing up. You don't have to use that," 00:09:26–00:09:31). It carries no criteria for how to know an athlete has met a stage's bar, no timelines, and no evidence it improves outcomes; it is a communication convention, not an assessment protocol. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's own testing and reassessment criteria (movement quality, injury history, training background, and phase-appropriate retesting) already govern this question [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment]; CM2 should not substitute for them.

**Example** — Weber's illustration: an athlete in early rehab who cannot yet sequence multiple joints stays in single-joint Control work (e.g., isolated clam exercises) rather than progressing to complex movement drills; once that control is established, the priority becomes "getting moving" as fast as safely possible rather than lingering in isolated work (00:07:07–00:07:44).

# The Decision Pathway: Six Stages, Five Gaps to Audit

**What it is** — Weber's model of the full route from an observation to an action: **data capture -> quality control -> analysis -> interpretation -> communication -> decision and action** (Video Lab 6D summary, 00:00–02:02). He names a specific gap between each pair of adjacent stages. **(1) Dirty data** (capture to quality control): check that the collection protocol was actually followed and that anomalies are caught before entering reports or a long-term database, with a named owner for the check. **(2) Expertise** (quality control to analysis): a reliable measurement can still be judged against an unsuitable threshold, or without its normal context, including software defaults that were never reviewed. **(3) Interpretation** (analysis to meaning): a number can reach a meeting with no one stating what it means for the athlete or the decision, and excess data can exceed the team's capacity to interpret it. **(4) Communication** (interpretation to decision-maker): technical language can obscure the actual requested action; Weber recommends leading with a clear recommendation and supplying supporting detail in a form the recipient can use. **(5) Authority** (recommendation to action): even a clear recommendation can be ignored without a formal decision gate or override process; he calls for explicit decision authority and a record of recommendations and decisions (02:02–10:50).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: pathways break "not because the people are bad at jobs, but the process has a gap. Steps are not defined and people's roles within those steps are not defined" (6D transcript 00:00:42 to 00:00:52), and naming the stages lets a team "name exactly where your pathway is breaking" (00:00:57 to 00:01:06). Inference: this is the same diagnostic logic as [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]], applied to a single decision's pipeline.

**When to apply** — Weber's own stated practical use: trace a recent important decision through all six stages, identify the gap that most affects decisions, and assign a concrete owner and process to close it (10:52–12:11). **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar) rather than by sport, with no sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently documented [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment; Load monitoring and GPS]. **Inference:** Weber's expertise-gap point, that someone needs to set and review the thresholds a measurement is judged against, including software defaults, lands directly on that named gap; this framework gives it a specific owner-and-process fix rather than leaving it as a general observation.

**When NOT to apply** — This framework audits the pipeline's structure; it does not itself validate whether a given threshold or software default is the right one, only that someone should be reviewing it. It also assumes a decision pathway already exists to be traced — for a genuinely new signal with no established pathway, the encoding and integration frameworks (see [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]]) are the prior step.

**Example** — Weber's communication-gap framing: leading with a clear recommendation first, and putting supporting technical detail in a form the recipient can actually use, rather than requiring the recipient to extract the recommendation from technical language themselves (05:32–08:54) — the same discipline as [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] applied specifically at the decision-pathway's communication stage.

**Related** — [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] — the department-level companion to this pipeline-level audit. [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — the communication-gap discipline this framework names as stage four. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the formal structure for stage five's authority and action.

# Evidence Stacking: Don't Decide on One Dramatic Signal

**What it is** — Weber's central question for any consequential decision, per the lesson summary: does staff have enough independent, relevant information to act (Podcast 2 summary, 00:00–02:20). A dramatic single result or first impression should prompt further investigation, not settle the decision. An evidence stack combines the event/problem history, clinical findings where relevant, the athlete's own prior results, movement and capacity checks, and performance under the conditions the decision actually concerns (00:00–02:20). His practical takeaway: define the decision first, identify the important unanswered questions, then choose measures that each add distinct evidence rather than repeating what is already known (17:35–18:15). This is the same caution Weber repeats in narrower form elsewhere in the course: in Lab 2A, one test returning to baseline is treated as one data point rather than a stand-alone clearance (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02); in Webinar 1 Part III, one favorable test result is not a complete return-to-running answer (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 07:44–08:54); and in Podcast 1, he warns specifically against treating a single red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated purpose, per the lesson summary, is to separate meaningful change from noise and to communicate decisions with appropriate confidence (Podcast 2 summary, 00:00–02:20). **Inference:** the likely reason combining sources helps is that different evidence types fail in different, largely independent ways: a single clinical impression, a single hop-test result, and a single speed-exposure metric can each individually mislead, but they are unlikely to all mislead in the same direction at once. Updating the working assessment as each new piece arrives, illustrated with Weber's soccer-knee and hamstring anecdotes (02:20–17:35), is more robust than treating any one piece as decisive.

**When to apply** — Any return-to-play, load, or selection decision where one metric alone is being used to justify the call, especially under time pressure or when a result is unusually dramatic (very good or very bad). **Eric's baseline:** the course transcripts in Eric's own corpus argue "you don't need a fancy test or anything to do that. But you do have to have a good coach's eye," while Eric's own SportSmith writing moved the opposite direction on daily monitoring by replacing subjective wellness surveys with objective mRSI [method-baseline.md Tensions #3]. **Inference:** evidence stacking offers a synthesis rather than forcing a choice between those two positions: the coach's eye is one more independent stream to stack alongside the objective metric, not a competitor to it.

**When NOT to apply** — Per the lesson summary's own caveat (not Weber's words), the anecdotes illustrate a reasoning approach and do not establish that a triple-hop baseline can diagnose a knee injury; medical diagnosis and clearance remain clinical decisions (Podcast 2 summary, practical takeaway). It also does not specify how many independent streams are enough for a given decision; that judgment is left to the practitioner.

**Example** — Weber's hamstring case: clinical progress and gym measures were supplemented with hopping, running-speed exposure, and a comparison of running mechanics at matched speeds, specifically to close the gap between controlled tests and actual field demands before returning the athlete to competition (Podcast 2 summary, 10:30–17:35). The reported outcome is one case, not a validated return-to-play rule. Untested anecdote (n=1). The mechanics comparison used SpeedSig, Weber's own product (Podcast 2 transcript 00:15:52 to 00:16:18); treat the case as an illustration by an interested party, not evidence for the product or the return pathway.

# The Integration Problem: Five Break Points Between Data and Decision

**What it is** — Weber's framework for a specific failure mode: a practitioner collects genuinely useful information, but it never influences a decision because the organization has no reliable way to interpret, discuss, or act on it. "Good information does not guarantee influence... this is usually not a knowledge problem" (The_Leader_s_Integration_Cheat_Sheet.pdf p.1). His five break points, tracing a signal from collection to action: **(1) language gap** — teams use different terms or underlying models for athlete status, readiness, risk, or rehabilitation; **(2) decision pathway gap** — no agreed route identifies who collects, reviews, discusses, and uses technical information, or what triggers a conversation; **(3) authority gradient** — a senior decision-maker can override a technical recommendation without discussion or explanation (Weber favors hearing competing cases and explaining the decision, rather than a silent override); **(4) relationship deficit** — the person who must act does not yet understand or trust the evidence; per the lesson summary, Weber frames this as a shared responsibility, with practitioners sharing responsibility for preparing colleagues to interpret new information; **(5) process absence** — missing meeting gates, decision checkpoints, or review steps let a team skip important intermediate judgments (Video Lab 6A summary, 06:58–13:14; cheat sheet p.1). His diagnostic test: "if your recommendation changes as it moves up the chain, there is likely an integration leak" (cheat sheet p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's core claim, stated directly, is that departments fail through structure, not intent: recommendations get ignored, diluted, or misunderstood because the environment lacks the pathway to handle them, not because the underlying analysis was wrong (cheat sheet p.1). **Inference:** naming five distinct break points turns a vague sense that good work isn't landing into a specific, auditable question, which of the five links actually failed.

**When to apply** — Reviewing a past decision where technically sound information did not change the outcome, or auditing a department's current pathway for a specific recurring signal (e.g., a fatigue flag, an asymmetry finding). Weber's own audit question directly names the exercise: "you need to ask whether your data has ever directly changed a major decision, and whether you can trace the path from collection to action" (cheat sheet p.1). **Eric's baseline:** KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing is named as a departmental operating principle, but no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in the reviewed corpus [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** Weber's audit question is a useful test to run against that specific gap.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own account of a past bone-stress-injury case, where he says he had not communicated his evidence in a form colleagues could use, is a personal anecdote illustrating the communication point; it does not establish a general injury-prediction rule from training surface, and the transcript cannot verify the causal claim (Video Lab 6A summary, 13:14–15:38). This framework also assumes the underlying information was sound in the first place; it diagnoses pathway failure, not measurement or inference failure (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] for that separate question).

**Example** — Weber's authority-gradient distinction: overriding a technical recommendation, in the course's words, "sometimes that is necessary, but it should happen transparently and with explanation" (cheat sheet p.1) — the failure mode is the silent override, not the override itself.

**Related** — [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]] — the next-stage problem (same information, different disciplinary lens) that this framework's language gap connects to. [[framework--decision-pathway-six-stages-five-gaps]] — a parallel, more granular breakdown of the data-to-decision pipeline. [[framework--grey-zone-overlap-ownership]] — where the authority gradient is resolved for medical/performance overlap specifically.

14	# The Knowledge x Behaviour Matrix
15	
16	**What it is** — A 2x2 grid Weber uses to discuss staff capability separately from staff engagement. The **knowledge axis** (horizontal): **handbrake** (insufficient or poorly aligned knowledge for the setting), **pawn** (fundamentals without complex problem-solving), **practitioner** (strong across domains, able to contribute), **operator** (broad knowledge, independent complex problem-solving) (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 07:35–10:00). The **behaviour axis** (vertical): **misaligned**, **coasting** (contributes in a stable role without pushing change), **catalyst** (proactively influences the team even without leading change alone), and **beacon** at the top of the range (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 10:00–11:57; Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 00:00–01:07). Weber is explicit these are role-capability labels, meant to describe knowledge and behaviour rather than to judge a person's overall worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10). A companion student worksheet (published under Weber's SpeedSig brand) operationalizes the grid as a self-audit: define both axes in your own words, self-place on each axis now and for a 3–5 year target, then map 3–5 colleagues onto the same categories using initials or role titles only (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, Sections A–C). The behaviour axis has four levels in the video (Webinar 1 Part II transcript 00:10:21 to 00:12:16: misaligned, coasting, catalyst, beacon) and in the Grey Zone Workbook p.2, but three in the Lab 1b blog and the student workbook (A3). Beacon is the top tier; the three-level handouts omit it.
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber gives the grid two uses: development (spot skill gaps, plan CPD: Lab 1B Part 2 summary 02:10 to 04:04) and selection (Lab 1B Part 1 transcript 00:07:40 to 00:08:02: misaligned staff "need to be managed out"; Lab_1b blog p.4: "Make tough calls on the misaligned"). **Inference:** splitting knowledge from behaviour also separates two different interventions, a low-knowledge/high-catalyst person likely needs training, while a high-knowledge/coasting person needs a different kind of push, consistent with Weber's own worked contrast (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Structuring a 1:1 development conversation, a hiring discussion, or a mentoring assignment where the real question is whether a person needs more knowledge, more engagement, or both. Weber's advice to pick a mentor above you who has worked in elite sport (Lab 1B Part 1 transcript, 06:10–07:07) is a direct extension of the knowledge axis; see [[heuristic--choose-a-mentor-above-you-who-has-worked-in-elite-sport]].
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this grid, or any output from the SpeedSig worksheet, to place a named Baylor colleague into a "handbrake" or "misaligned" category in any written record; Weber's own framing is explicit that the grid is meant to evaluate knowledge and behavior, not a person's overall worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10), and the course's own worksheet instructs anonymizing colleagues by role title for exactly this reason. It is also entirely self- or supervisor-report, with no validation evidence that placement on the grid predicts performance or that movement between quadrants is trainable on any particular timeline. Inference: any real personnel decision would still need direct evidence, fair process and Baylor HR policy (the lesson summary adds the same caveat).
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own worked contrast: someone with limited knowledge but strong initiative may be worth developing, while deep expertise paired with little engagement can hold a team's progress back (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).
25	
26	**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] and [[heuristic--choose-a-mentor-above-you-who-has-worked-in-elite-sport]] — the two concrete practices Weber pairs with this matrix.
27

14	# Measurement vs. Inference
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's distinction between what a tool actually captures (a **measurement**: force, distance, speed, displacement) and the explanation applied to that output (an **inference**: fatigue, tissue status, readiness) (Lab 2A summary, 00:00–01:45). His examples, per the lesson summary: calling a lower countermovement-jump result neurological fatigue, or a GPS change tissue stress — neither label follows directly from the measurement alone, and athletes can produce a similar output through a different movement strategy, so a stable score can hide a real change in mechanics (01:45–03:20). 14	# Name the Meeting Mode Before You Set the Agenda: Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's four meeting modes, each with a different structure and expected output. **Decide**: a clear question with limited options, using pre-reading, time-boxed input, an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review — the same structure as the kaigi format (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14; see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]). **Diagnose**: a known problem whose cause or solution is uncertain, gathering perspectives and hypotheses on a defined problem with time-boxed contributions (Weber's example: roughly 30 minutes), assigning a smaller group to gather more information if unresolved, then scheduling a later decision (02:14–04:03). **Inform**: sharing updates and context, with an explicit warning that inform meetings can drift into unplanned problem-solving if not held to that purpose (04:37–05:02). **Build**: co-creating or redesigning a system, structure, or training week, giving people room to contribute, considering psychological safety, and allowing time to digest ideas across possibly several meetings rather than forcing one immediate decision (05:34–06:18). Weber also names two composite formats: an **operations meeting** (brief status updates, blocker removal, ownership assignment, combining informing with quick decisions, 05:02–05:34) and a **retrospective/after-action review** (a factual, blameless timeline of what happened, using measures and named gaps, translated into procedure changes, 06:18–07:08). His practical rule: for each agenda item, write one verb — decide, diagnose, inform, or build — plus the question, expected output, time limit, and pre-reading (07:08–08:09).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: naming the mode in advance tells participants what kind of contribution is needed and protects creative or diagnostic work from being cut short by premature decision pressure, while letting genuinely decidable questions move fast once the options are known. A single staff meeting can move through several modes in sequence, provided each segment states its own purpose and output so participants know which mode they are in at any given moment (04:03–04:37).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Building or reviewing any recurring departmental meeting's agenda, or diagnosing why a specific meeting series feels unproductive (often because it is running **decide** structure on a **diagnose** problem, or vice versa). **Eric's baseline:** the course team's material treats the annual plan as a roadmap adapted as circumstances change [method-baseline.md line 149, Inferred]. **Inference:** the baseline records no after-action or retrospective format, so the AAR mode (cheat sheet p.2: 15 to 30 min, blameless, learning points plus procedure changes plus owners) would be new practice at Baylor, not a formalization of an existing one.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no evidence that naming a mode improves meeting outcomes beyond his own stated experience; this is a proposed practice, not a tested intervention. It also does not resolve who decides which mode an agenda item needs; that judgment is left to whoever sets the agenda. Inference: a leader who uses a meeting to gather perspectives that test their own initial view before deciding (07:08–08:09) is deliberately using diagnose-mode dynamics inside what will eventually become a decide-mode outcome, a legitimate but easily-missed hybrid use.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's retrospective example, per the lesson summary: reviewing a run of injuries with a factual timeline and named missing information, kept blameless, then translated into a procedure change rather than a verdict on any individual (06:18–07:08).
25

13	
14	# Monitoring vs. Testing
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's separation of two questions that are often mashed together. **Monitoring** answers "has something changed right now," sits on a days-to-weeks horizon, and is "status and trend": day-to-day jump performance, session exposure/tolerance, readiness markers, short-term fatigue signals, feeding load adjustments, recovery decisions, and progression/regression calls (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1). **Testing** answers "have we improved capacity across a training phase," sits on a weeks-to-months horizon, and is "progress": pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two, evaluating whether the program is working (p.1). His explicit warning: short-term monitoring methods (rolling averages, exponentially weighted moving averages) are built to detect drift from a recent baseline, not to answer whether capacity improved across a training phase — "different questions require different analysis" (p.1–2). His communication checklist for either one: state what is being evaluated, why, how often, what output the coach will receive, and what different results would trigger, before pressure to act arrives (p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's own stated point is that different questions require different analysis (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). **Inference:** a rolling baseline moves with the athlete, so it can hide a slow, real change in capacity even while flagging every short-term dip; conversely, comparing two widely separated phase blocks would not catch a same-week acute status change. Using the wrong analysis method for the question likely produces a plausible-looking number that answers a different question than the one being asked.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Whenever a metric is being tracked at both a daily/weekly cadence and used to make phase-level claims about program effectiveness. **Eric's baseline:** the baseline states a preference for weekly tracking over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment]. **Inference:** this is a real tension worth naming: Weber's framework would say that weekly cadence is monitoring (a status/trend check), and it still needs a separate, phase-block comparison to answer the testing question of whether the athlete actually improved. The two are not substitutes for each other even when the same test (e.g., daily CMJ for mRSI) feeds both.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Inference: single-number illustrations in the course, such as the 12% RFD change Weber dismisses as "well inside our range of variability with the MDC" (Lab 2E transcript 00:04:08 to 00:04:24), are local examples, not transferable thresholds; the lesson summary adds the same caveat (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]). This framework also does not resolve which specific quality to monitor or test for a given sport — that is the prior question in [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]].
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's decision-matrix template: "if we get this result, we do these steps, owned by these people, reviewed at this time point," worked through for an eccentric-knee-flexor-force drop (confirm test quality/re-test, physio screen and ROM checks, adjust exposure plan, reassess immediately and at 24 hours, progress only when stable) (p.2).
25	
26	**Related** — [[heuristic--rolling-baselines-miss-gradual-drift]] — the specific failure mode this framework warns against.
