# The Knowledge x Behaviour Matrix

**What it is** — A 2x2 grid Weber uses to discuss staff capability separately from staff engagement. The **knowledge axis** (horizontal): **handbrake** (insufficient or poorly aligned knowledge for the setting), **pawn** (fundamentals without complex problem-solving), **practitioner** (strong across domains, able to contribute), **operator** (broad knowledge, independent complex problem-solving) (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 07:35–10:00). The **behaviour axis** (vertical): **misaligned**, **coasting** (contributes in a stable role without pushing change), **catalyst** (proactively influences the team even without leading change alone), and **beacon** at the top of the range (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 10:00–11:57; Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 00:00–01:07). Weber is explicit these are role-capability labels, meant to describe knowledge and behaviour rather than to judge a person's overall worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10). A companion student worksheet (published under Weber's SpeedSig brand) operationalizes the grid as a self-audit: define both axes in your own words, self-place on each axis now and for a 3–5 year target, then map 3–5 colleagues onto the same categories using initials or role titles only (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, Sections A–C). The behaviour axis has four levels in the video (Webinar 1 Part II transcript 00:10:21 to 00:12:16: misaligned, coasting, catalyst, beacon) and in the Grey Zone Workbook p.2, but three in the Lab 1b blog and the student workbook (A3). Beacon is the top tier; the three-level handouts omit it.

**Why it works** — Weber gives the grid two uses: development (spot skill gaps, plan CPD: Lab 1B Part 2 summary 02:10 to 04:04) and selection (Lab 1B Part 1 transcript 00:07:40 to 00:08:02: misaligned staff "need to be managed out"; Lab_1b blog p.4: "Make tough calls on the misaligned"). **Inference:** splitting knowledge from behaviour also separates two different interventions, a low-knowledge/high-catalyst person likely needs training, while a high-knowledge/coasting person needs a different kind of push, consistent with Weber's own worked contrast (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).

**When to apply** — Structuring a 1:1 development conversation, a hiring discussion, or a mentoring assignment where the real question is whether a person needs more knowledge, more engagement, or both. Weber's advice to pick a mentor above you who has worked in elite sport (Lab 1B Part 1 transcript, 06:10–07:07) is a direct extension of the knowledge axis; see [[heuristic--choose-a-mentor-above-you-who-has-worked-in-elite-sport]].

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this grid, or any output from the SpeedSig worksheet, to place a named Baylor colleague into a "handbrake" or "misaligned" category in any written record; Weber's own framing is explicit that the grid is meant to evaluate knowledge and behavior, not a person's overall worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10), and the course's own worksheet instructs anonymizing colleagues by role title for exactly this reason. It is also entirely self- or supervisor-report, with no validation evidence that placement on the grid predicts performance or that movement between quadrants is trainable on any particular timeline. Inference: any real personnel decision would still need direct evidence, fair process and Baylor HR policy (the lesson summary adds the same caveat).

**Example** — Weber's own worked contrast: someone with limited knowledge but strong initiative may be worth developing, while deep expertise paired with little engagement can hold a team's progress back (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).

**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] and [[heuristic--choose-a-mentor-above-you-who-has-worked-in-elite-sport]] — the two concrete practices Weber pairs with this matrix.

# Measurement vs. Inference

**What it is** — Weber's distinction between what a tool actually captures (a **measurement**: force, distance, speed, displacement) and the explanation applied to that output (an **inference**: fatigue, tissue status, readiness) (Lab 2A summary, 00:00–01:45). His examples, per the lesson summary: calling a lower countermovement-jump result neurological fatigue, or a GPS change tissue stress — neither label follows directly from the measurement alone, and athletes can produce a similar output through a different movement strategy, so a stable score can hide a real change in mechanics (01:45–03:20). His stated communication rule: report what was measured, identify what is being inferred, state your confidence in that inference, and recommend the next exposure or check (05:02–06:02).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated reasons: overstating certainty "is what drives coaches crazy" (Lab_2a PDF p.2; transcript 00:02:09 to 00:02:17), and because "humans are an incredibly redundant system" the same output can hide different strategies (Lab_2a PDF p.2), so an inference has to be built by triangulation to a probability, not asserted (PDF p.3; transcript 00:03:20 to 00:04:01). **Inference:** collapsing the distinction likely lets a causal story ride along silently with a number, so the story gets treated with the same confidence as the measurement itself. Naming the inference as an inference forces an explicit confidence statement instead of an implicit one, and makes the underlying reasoning available for someone else to challenge.

**When to apply** — Any report or conversation where a device output is being used to say something about the athlete's internal state (fatigue, readiness, tissue tolerance) rather than just the output itself. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring]. **Inference:** this framework's discipline would ask the same question of mRSI that Weber asks of his CMJ example, what is actually measured (jump-derived force/time output), and what is being inferred from it (neuromuscular readiness), stated with what confidence.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication and reasoning discipline, not a claim that inference is unreliable or should be avoided; Weber's own examples (hamstring context: injury history, strength tests, jumping/hopping, speed exposure, running mechanics) show that combining several measurements to support one inference is the intended use, not a replacement for inference altogether (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02). It also does not by itself tell you whether an observed change exceeds measurement noise — see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question.

**Example** — Weber treats one test returning to baseline as one data point, not a stand-alone clearance, in his hamstring illustration (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02) — the same discipline generalized into a full framework in [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]].

**Related** — [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — combining multiple inferences before acting on any one of them. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — whether the measurement itself is trustworthy before it is interpreted. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]] — the upstream discipline of naming the question before choosing what to measure.

# Name the Meeting Mode Before You Set the Agenda: Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build

**What it is** — Weber's four meeting modes, each with a different structure and expected output. **Decide**: a clear question with limited options, using pre-reading, time-boxed input, an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review — the same structure as the kaigi format (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14; see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]). **Diagnose**: a known problem whose cause or solution is uncertain, gathering perspectives and hypotheses on a defined problem with time-boxed contributions (Weber's example: roughly 30 minutes), assigning a smaller group to gather more information if unresolved, then scheduling a later decision (02:14–04:03). **Inform**: sharing updates and context, with an explicit warning that inform meetings can drift into unplanned problem-solving if not held to that purpose (04:37–05:02). **Build**: co-creating or redesigning a system, structure, or training week, giving people room to contribute, considering psychological safety, and allowing time to digest ideas across possibly several meetings rather than forcing one immediate decision (05:34–06:18). Weber also names two composite formats: an **operations meeting** (brief status updates, blocker removal, ownership assignment, combining informing with quick decisions, 05:02–05:34) and a **retrospective/after-action review** (a factual, blameless timeline of what happened, using measures and named gaps, translated into procedure changes, 06:18–07:08). His practical rule: for each agenda item, write one verb — decide, diagnose, inform, or build — plus the question, expected output, time limit, and pre-reading (07:08–08:09).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: naming the mode in advance tells participants what kind of contribution is needed and protects creative or diagnostic work from being cut short by premature decision pressure, while letting genuinely decidable questions move fast once the options are known. A single staff meeting can move through several modes in sequence, provided each segment states its own purpose and output so participants know which mode they are in at any given moment (04:03–04:37).

**When to apply** — Building or reviewing any recurring departmental meeting's agenda, or diagnosing why a specific meeting series feels unproductive (often because it is running **decide** structure on a **diagnose** problem, or vice versa). **Eric's baseline:** the course team's material treats the annual plan as a roadmap adapted as circumstances change [method-baseline.md line 149, Inferred]. **Inference:** the baseline records no after-action or retrospective format, so the AAR mode (cheat sheet p.2: 15 to 30 min, blameless, learning points plus procedure changes plus owners) would be new practice at Baylor, not a formalization of an existing one.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no evidence that naming a mode improves meeting outcomes beyond his own stated experience; this is a proposed practice, not a tested intervention. It also does not resolve who decides which mode an agenda item needs; that judgment is left to whoever sets the agenda. Inference: a leader who uses a meeting to gather perspectives that test their own initial view before deciding (07:08–08:09) is deliberately using diagnose-mode dynamics inside what will eventually become a decide-mode outcome, a legitimate but easily-missed hybrid use.

**Example** — Weber's retrospective example, per the lesson summary: reviewing a run of injuries with a factual timeline and named missing information, kept blameless, then translated into a procedure change rather than a verdict on any individual (06:18–07:08).

**Related** — [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]] — the fuller **decide**-mode structure. [[framework--stoplight-storytelling-format]] — a presentation format built for the **decide** mode specifically. [[heuristic--time-box-recurring-meetings]] — the time-discipline this typology assumes throughout.

# Name the Meeting Mode Before You Set the Agenda: Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build

**What it is** — Weber's four meeting modes, each with a different structure and expected output. **Decide**: a clear question with limited options, using pre-reading, time-boxed input, an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review: the same structure as the kaigi format (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14; see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]). **Diagnose**: a known problem whose cause or solution is uncertain, gathering perspectives and hypotheses on a defined problem with time-boxed contributions (Weber's example: roughly 30 minutes), assigning a smaller group to gather more information if unresolved, then scheduling a later decision (02:14–04:03). **Inform**: sharing updates and context, with an explicit warning that inform meetings can drift into unplanned problem-solving if not held to that purpose (04:37–05:02). **Build**: co-creating or redesigning a system, structure, or training week, giving people room to contribute, considering psychological safety, and allowing time to digest ideas across possibly several meetings rather than forcing one immediate decision (05:34–06:18). Weber also names two composite formats: an **operations meeting** (brief status updates, blocker removal, ownership assignment, combining informing with quick decisions, 05:02–05:34) and a **retrospective/after-action review** (a factual, blameless timeline of what happened, using measures and named gaps, translated into procedure changes, 06:18–07:08). His practical rule: for each agenda item, write one verb — decide, diagnose, inform, or build — plus the question, expected output, time limit, and pre-reading (07:08–08:09).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: naming the mode in advance tells participants what kind of contribution is needed and protects creative or diagnostic work from being cut short by premature decision pressure, while letting genuinely decidable questions move fast once the options are known. A single staff meeting can move through several modes in sequence, provided each segment states its own purpose and output so participants know which mode they are in at any given moment (04:03–04:37).

**When to apply** — Building or reviewing any recurring departmental meeting's agenda, or diagnosing why a specific meeting series feels unproductive (often because it is running **decide** structure on a **diagnose** problem, or vice versa). **Eric's baseline:** the course team's material treats the annual plan as a roadmap adapted as circumstances change [method-baseline.md line 149, Inferred]. **Inference:** the baseline records no after-action or retrospective format, so the AAR mode (cheat sheet p.2: 15 to 30 min, blameless, learning points plus procedure changes plus owners) would be new practice at Baylor, not a formalization of an existing one.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no evidence that naming a mode improves meeting outcomes beyond his own stated experience; this is a proposed practice, not a tested intervention. It also does not resolve who decides which mode an agenda item needs; that judgment is left to whoever sets the agenda. Inference: a leader who uses a meeting to gather perspectives that test their own initial view before deciding (07:08–08:09) is deliberately using diagnose-mode dynamics inside what will eventually become a decide-mode outcome, a legitimate but easily-missed hybrid use.

**Example** — Weber's retrospective example, per the lesson summary: reviewing a run of injuries with a factual timeline and named missing information, kept blameless, then translated into a procedure change rather than a verdict on any individual (06:18–07:08).

# Monitoring vs. Testing

**What it is** — Weber's separation of two questions that are often mashed together. **Monitoring** answers "has something changed right now," sits on a days-to-weeks horizon, and is "status and trend": day-to-day jump performance, session exposure/tolerance, readiness markers, short-term fatigue signals, feeding load adjustments, recovery decisions, and progression/regression calls (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1). **Testing** answers "have we improved capacity across a training phase," sits on a weeks-to-months horizon, and is "progress": pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two, evaluating whether the program is working (p.1). His explicit warning: short-term monitoring methods (rolling averages, exponentially weighted moving averages) are built to detect drift from a recent baseline, not to answer whether capacity improved across a training phase — "different questions require different analysis" (p.1–2). His communication checklist for either one: state what is being evaluated, why, how often, what output the coach will receive, and what different results would trigger, before pressure to act arrives (p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated point is that different questions require different analysis (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). **Inference:** a rolling baseline moves with the athlete, so it can hide a slow, real change in capacity even while flagging every short-term dip; conversely, comparing two widely separated phase blocks would not catch a same-week acute status change. Using the wrong analysis method for the question likely produces a plausible-looking number that answers a different question than the one being asked.

**When to apply** — Whenever a metric is being tracked at both a daily/weekly cadence and used to make phase-level claims about program effectiveness. **Eric's baseline:** the baseline states a preference for weekly tracking over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment]. **Inference:** this is a real tension worth naming: Weber's framework would say that weekly cadence is monitoring (a status/trend check), and it still needs a separate, phase-block comparison to answer the testing question of whether the athlete actually improved. The two are not substitutes for each other even when the same test (e.g., daily CMJ for mRSI) feeds both.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: single-number illustrations in the course, such as the 12% RFD change Weber dismisses as "well inside our range of variability with the MDC" (Lab 2E transcript 00:04:08 to 00:04:24), are local examples, not transferable thresholds; the lesson summary adds the same caveat (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]). This framework also does not resolve which specific quality to monitor or test for a given sport — that is the prior question in [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]].

**Example** — Weber's decision-matrix template: "if we get this result, we do these steps, owned by these people, reviewed at this time point," worked through for an eccentric-knee-flexor-force drop (confirm test quality/re-test, physio screen and ROM checks, adjust exposure plan, reassess immediately and at 24 hours, progress only when stable) (p.2).

**Related** — [[heuristic--rolling-baselines-miss-gradual-drift]] — the specific failure mode this framework warns against. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the formal structure for the "if this, then that" decision matrix Weber describes here. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]] — the shared "name the quality first" operating principle.

14	# System Reliability vs. Individual Sensitivity: ICC, SEM, MDC, and SWC
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber separates two questions that a decision gate's criteria depend on. **System-level reliability** ("can we trust the test at all") covers the whole system, not just the device: equipment, protocol, tester, environment, athlete execution. Its tools: **ICC** (intraclass correlation coefficient, how consistently athletes are ranked across repeated trials — relative reliability), **SEM/TE** (standard error of measurement / typical error, the size of the noise in real units — absolute reliability), and **MDC95** (minimal detectable change, how much change is needed to be confident a shift exceeds typical noise at high confidence) (Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf p.1). **Individual-level monitoring sensitivity** ("can we detect meaningful change in this athlete") uses within-athlete typical error or coefficient of variation (CV%) to define **SWC** (smallest worthwhile change: the smallest change that is practically meaningful, not just statistically real) (p.1). His key distinction: "MDC answers: is it beyond noise? SWC answers: is it worth caring about?" — both matter, and they serve different purposes (p.1). 14	# Judge a Technology by Its Adoption Stage, Not Just Its Existence
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber applies Rogers' innovation-adoption curve to performance technology: a tool's usefulness to a given department depends on where it sits on the maturity curve (early/skeptical adopters through mainstream use), not just on whether it exists or is popular elsewhere. His example: GPS moved from being met with skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: the curve "helps us understand how technology will be adopted and utilised within our environment", and staff knowledge and behaviour set how far up it a department can go (Webinar 1 Part II transcript 00:07:08 to 00:07:35). **Inference:** adopting before procedures and staff skill have matured likely recreates the tech-rich, procedure-poor problem (Lab_1c PDF p.1), the tool exists, but the surrounding discipline needed to use it well does not yet exist; see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]].
19	
20	**When to apply** — Weighing a genuinely new technology (a novel wearable, an AI-based analysis tool) against an established one with known error, interpretation norms, and staff familiarity. The question this framework poses is not whether the tool is valid in principle, but whether the tool, and the staff's ability to use it, have matured to the point where adopting it now is worth the transition cost.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for placing a specific tool on the curve, and the maturity claim here is his own retrospective narrative about GPS, not a measured or validated adoption metric for any other technology. It should not be read as an argument to always wait for mainstream adoption. **Inference:** earlier-stage tools can still be worth adopting deliberately, with the added discipline that comes with being an early user.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's GPS timeline, per the lesson summary: he contrasts early adopters of new tools with GPS specifically, which he says moved from skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35). This is his personal recollection, not a documented industry history in this corpus. His other illustration is his own product, SpeedSig, placed at the innovator stage (00:05:16 to 00:05:45); an interested party's example.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit that reveals whether a department's procedures have caught up to a tool it already owns.

13	
14	# Stoplight Storytelling
15	
16	**What it is** — A short, repeatable presentation format for bringing a decision to a group: state the question or headline first (rather than opening with data that has no stated purpose); show status using green (go), amber (hold/monitor), or red (stop/change); present at most one chart, readable immediately, that addresses whether an observed difference is meaningful relative to measurement error, normal variation, and other convergent evidence; and close with a requested direction (start/stop/change) plus one owner, one action, a due date, and a review point recorded in the decision log (Lab 3C summary, 00:00–04:25; see [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]). Presentation rules: keep the message short, label axes and differences clearly, avoid dual axes and complex charts that require extended explanation, never bring multiple charts, multiple requests, or brand-new information into the moment, and give every status, including amber, a next action or review date (04:25–06:23). A roughly two-minute presentation is Weber's own benchmark, though he notes novel or complex issues may need pre-reading or a separate meeting instead (06:23–06:43). Timing is given two ways: about two minutes per slide (3C transcript 00:06:23 to 00:06:28; template p.2; cheat sheet p.2 "2 min per slide") and about five minutes per person, five presentations in 30 minutes (00:07:30 to 00:07:38).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated purpose, per the lesson summary, is to keep a sequence of presentations in one meeting from expanding into long, unfocused discussions, and to let staff present more autonomously once the shared format is understood (06:56–07:54). **Inference:** forcing one chart and one request likely removes the two most common ways a presentation drifts, adding more evidence than the room can process in the time available, and leaving the ask implicit so no decision actually gets made.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any recurring review where multiple practitioners each need to bring a status update that may require a decision: a weekly return-to-play review, a load-monitoring standup, or a technology-adoption check-in. Pairs directly with the kaigi format's evidence-precision rule (see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]) as the visual layer of the same discipline.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber's two-minute benchmark and single-chart rule are explicitly not meant for novel or complex issues, which he says may need pre-reading or a dedicated meeting instead (06:23–06:43); **Inference:** forcing a genuinely complex, multi-variable problem into stoplight format would risk the same false simplicity the framework is otherwise designed to avoid (see [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]]). The timing and efficiency claims are Weber's own practice examples, not validated thresholds.
23	
24	**Example** — The course's slide template (Lab_3c_Stoplight_Storytelling_Slide_Template.pdf p.1 to p.2): headline decision question; one stoplight status with a one-line reason; one chart with baseline, current, change, SEM and MDC95; at most two pieces of convergent evidence; one ask written as a verb (Start/Stop/Change/Limit/Continue); owner, action, due, review; footer "2 minutes total. If it needs explaining, it's the wrong meeting type."
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]] — the closing record this format requires. [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]] — the meeting format this presentation style is built to feed. [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — the caution against over-simplifying a genuinely complex decision.
27

13	
14	# Strategy Is the Highway, Tactics Are Changing Lanes
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's delegation model: **strategy** is the department's direction, standards, and the key questions it cares about, described as "the highway"; **tactics** are the day-to-day choices staff make within that direction (which tool to deploy, how to adjust tests, timing, and exposure, how to respond to what they see), described as "changing lanes" (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1–2). The stated goal is to give staff tactical freedom while the leader maintains strategic alignment (p.2). He restates the same model in Webinar 3 Part III as a direct delegation rule: the leader names the destination and boundaries, staff choose tactics within them, with more discretion given to an experienced colleague than a new hire, and explicit criteria for which decisions must be escalated (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 03:56–06:30).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's own stated goal is that the model gives staff tactical freedom while the leader maintains strategic alignment (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.2). Weber's stated mechanism: clear intent lets staff know "what can I make a decision on and what do I need to push up the chain", and staff without direction "become disillusioned. Their behavior will change", while micromanagement costs the leader control of time (Webinar 3 Part III transcript 00:05:18 to 00:06:30).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Structuring how much autonomy a staff member has over test selection, session adjustments, or reporting choices, especially as a department scales past a size where informal alignment happens naturally. **Eric's baseline:** the Playbook's stated peer-department framing for Applied Performance ("enabling" other departments to answer their own questions) is not fully reconciled with a support-staff framing that also appears in the same corpus ("helping program and plan the training") [method-baseline.md Tensions #2]. **Inference:** naming the specific highway (standards, questions Applied Performance owns) versus the lanes (tactical choices left to individual practitioners) is a direct way to resolve that ambiguity in practice.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no method for determining where the highway's boundaries should sit for a given department or decision type; that judgment call is left entirely to the leader. It is also not a substitute for the formal escalation criteria a decision gate provides (see [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]) when the stakes are high enough to need a documented pass/fail/borderline threshold rather than a general delegation boundary.
23	
24	**Example** — A first-year graduate gets "one or two lanes max"; a 10-year colleague gets "the full six lane highway" (Webinar 3 Part III transcript 00:04:38 to 00:04:51; Lab_3D blog p.1: "six-lane highway ... but nobody drives off-road").
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]] — the audit this delegation model is embedded in. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the more formal structure for higher-stakes decisions. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]] — the companion communication rules from the same Webinar 3 material.

13	
14	# The Tech Stack Reality Check
15	
16	**What it is** — A three-step audit for an existing department, done before buying anything new. Step 1: inventory what you have **as measurement systems, not brands** ("people say 'we're doing NordBord.' NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength," Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). Weber's named categories: your computer (spreadsheets vs. real analysis/dashboard/coding capability), wearables (GNSS/GPS + IMU, not just "GPS"), force plates (force over time, not "jump height machines"), force transducers/load cells (isometrics, Nordics, dynamometry, where "if your setup changes, your test changes"), and linear position transducers (GymAware/FLEX-style, which need standardized naming, setup, ROM rules, and reporting rules) (pp.1–3). Step 2: for each measurement, establish **reliability** — can you repeat the number within a known error band, both within-session and between-session (p.3; Lab 1C transcript 00:03:47–00:04:45). Step 3: write down the **procedure** (warm-up, familiarization, instructions, trial structure) for at least one tool, because "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures... a procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:04:45–00:05:02; PDF p.3).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's argument is that many performance environments are "tech-rich and procedure-poor" (PDF p.1), which produces noise and decisions that feel like guesswork. Confusing a brand for the underlying test hides what is actually being measured; skipping reliability means a department will, in his words, "chase noise and call it insight" (PDF p.3) the first time two measurements disagree.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Before adding new technology, and as a standing onboarding document for new staff ("if you started a job this week... you need to be able to set standards for your staff to follow," Lab 1C transcript 00:05:07–00:05:29). **Eric's baseline:** documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting), except for the Catapult workflow, which has genuine operational depth [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2]. **Inference:** this audit's Step 1-3 sequence is a concrete way to close that gap tool by tool.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — This is a starting-point audit, not a statistics course; it names ICC/typical-error-style reliability concepts only in passing (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the fuller treatment). # The Tech Stack Reality Check

**What it is** — A three-step audit for an existing department, done before buying anything new. Step 1: inventory what you have **as measurement systems, not brands** ("people say 'we're doing NordBord.' NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength," Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). Weber's named categories: your computer (spreadsheets vs. real analysis/dashboard/coding capability), wearables (GNSS/GPS + IMU, not just "GPS"), force plates (force over time, not "jump height machines"), force transducers/load cells (isometrics, Nordics, dynamometry, where "if your setup changes, your test changes"), and linear position transducers (GymAware/FLEX-style, which need standardized naming, setup, ROM rules, and reporting rules) (pp.1–3). Step 2: for each measurement, establish **reliability** — can you repeat the number within a known error band, both within-session and between-session (p.3; Lab 1C transcript 00:03:47–00:04:45). Step 3: write down the **procedure** (warm-up, familiarization, instructions, trial structure) for at least one tool, because "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures... a procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:04:45–00:05:02; PDF p.3).

**Why it works** — Weber's argument is that many performance environments are "tech-rich and procedure-poor" (PDF p.1), which produces noise and decisions that feel like guesswork. Confusing a brand for the underlying test hides what is actually being measured; skipping reliability means a department will, in his words, "chase noise and call it insight" (PDF p.3) the first time two measurements disagree.

**When to apply** — Before adding new technology, and as a standing onboarding document for new staff ("if you started a job this week... you need to be able to set standards for your staff to follow," Lab 1C transcript 00:05:07–00:05:29). **Eric's baseline:** documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting), except for the Catapult workflow, which has genuine operational depth [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2]. **Inference:** this audit's Step 1-3 sequence is a concrete way to close that gap tool by tool.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a starting-point audit, not a statistics course; it names ICC/typical-error-style reliability concepts only in passing (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the fuller treatment). It also assumes a department already owns the technology being audited; it is not a tool-selection or purchasing framework, and it takes no position on which tools are worth owning in the first place.

**Example** — Weber's own admission that most practitioners "treat their laptop like a typewriter" (Lab_1c PDF p.1) and his contrast with himself ("Now that's me because I want to know and I want to be able to push myself further up the chain") illustrates the audit's first, most-overlooked category: the computer itself as a performance tool (Lab 1C transcript 00:01:13–00:02:32; see [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]]).

# System Reliability vs. Individual Sensitivity: ICC, SEM, MDC, and SWC

**What it is** — Weber separates two questions that a decision gate's criteria depend on. **System-level reliability** ("can we trust the test at all") covers the whole system, not just the device: equipment, protocol, tester, environment, athlete execution. Its tools: **ICC** (intraclass correlation coefficient, how consistently athletes are ranked across repeated trials — relative reliability), **SEM/TE** (standard error of measurement / typical error, the size of the noise in real units — absolute reliability), and **MDC95** (minimal detectable change, how much change is needed to be confident a shift exceeds typical noise at high confidence) (Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf p.1). **Individual-level monitoring sensitivity** ("can we detect meaningful change in this athlete") uses within-athlete typical error or coefficient of variation (CV%) to define **SWC** (smallest worthwhile change: the smallest change that is practically meaningful, not just statistically real) (p.1). His key distinction: "MDC answers: is it beyond noise? SWC answers: is it worth caring about?" — both matter, and they serve different purposes (p.1). His combined decision logic: change below MDC95 is likely noise; above MDC95, likely real; above SWC, likely meaningful; above both, act with confidence; real but not meaningful, note and watch without overreacting (p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's argument: "technology doesn't become valuable because it measures something. It becomes valuable when you can answer one question with confidence: is this change real, or is it noise?" (p.1). Without an MDC/SWC ladder, every observed change looks equally actionable, and a decision gate's pass/fail/borderline criteria (see [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]) have no defensible basis.

**When to apply** — Setting or reviewing the numeric threshold behind any decision gate, and specifically before trusting a daily readiness metric enough to act on small day-to-day changes in it. **Eric's baseline:** mRSI from daily CMJ is the department's chosen readiness marker, described as "objective, consistent, and actionable" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring]. **Inference:** the baseline records no MDC95, SWC or typical-error value for mRSI; Weber's framework would treat that missing figure as the non-negotiable step before any single-day mRSI change is used to make a training-load call.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber says elsewhere in the course that "you don't need to become a statistician" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2), and the same restraint applies here: the minimum thinking is required, not a full statistics course. This framework does not supply Baylor-specific ICC/SEM/MDC/SWC values for any test, only the structure for deriving and using them. Per the lesson summary's caveat (not Weber's words), the 12% figure and the MDC/SWC ladder are heuristics; the right calculation depends on the test and context (Lab 2E summary).

**Example** — Weber's RFD case: a physiotherapist reports an athlete's RFD is "off by 12%", which Weber calls "well inside our range of variability with the MDC" (Lab 2E transcript 00:04:08 to 00:04:24). The PDF gives the general point without a number: RFD is noisy because of execution consistency, onset detection and timing (Lab_2E PDF p.2); see [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] for his recommended response.

**Related** — [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the gate structure this statistics package supports. # System Reliability vs. Individual Sensitivity: ICC, SEM, MDC, and SWC

**What it is** — Weber separates two questions that a decision gate's criteria depend on. **System-level reliability** ("can we trust the test at all") covers the whole system, not just the device: equipment, protocol, tester, environment, athlete execution. Its tools: **ICC** (intraclass correlation coefficient: how consistently athletes are ranked across repeated trials, relative reliability), **SEM/TE** (standard error of measurement / typical error: the size of the noise in real units, absolute reliability), and **MDC95** (minimal detectable change, how much change is needed to be confident a shift exceeds typical noise at high confidence) (Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf p.1). **Individual-level monitoring sensitivity** ("can we detect meaningful change in this athlete") uses within-athlete typical error or coefficient of variation (CV%) to define **SWC** (smallest worthwhile change: the smallest change that is practically meaningful, not just statistically real) (p.1). His key distinction: "MDC answers: is it beyond noise? SWC answers: is it worth caring about?"; both matter, and they serve different purposes (p.1). His combined decision logic: change below MDC95 is likely noise; above MDC95, likely real; above SWC, likely meaningful; above both, act with confidence; real but not meaningful, note and watch without overreacting (p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's argument: "technology doesn't become valuable because it measures something. It becomes valuable when you can answer one question with confidence: is this change real, or is it noise?" (p.1). Without an MDC/SWC ladder, every observed change looks equally actionable, and a decision gate's pass/fail/borderline criteria (see [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]) have no defensible basis.

**When to apply** — Setting or reviewing the numeric threshold behind any decision gate, and specifically before trusting a daily readiness metric enough to act on small day-to-day changes in it. **Eric's baseline:** mRSI from daily CMJ is the department's chosen readiness marker, described as "objective, consistent, and actionable" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring]. **Inference:** the baseline records no MDC95, SWC or typical-error value for mRSI; Weber's framework would treat that missing figure as the non-negotiable step before any single-day mRSI change is used to make a training-load call.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber says elsewhere in the course that "you don't need to become a statistician" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2), and the same restraint applies here: the minimum thinking is required, not a full statistics course. This framework does not supply Baylor-specific ICC/SEM/MDC/SWC values for any test, only the structure for deriving and using them. Per the lesson summary's caveat (not Weber's words), the 12% figure and the MDC/SWC ladder are heuristics; the right calculation depends on the test and context (Lab 2E summary).

**Example** — Weber's RFD case: a physiotherapist reports an athlete's RFD is "off by 12%", which Weber calls "well inside our range of variability with the MDC" (Lab 2E transcript 00:04:08 to 00:04:24). The PDF gives the general point without a number: RFD is noisy because of execution consistency, onset detection and timing (Lab_2E PDF p.2); see [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] for his recommended response.

# Judge a Technology by Its Adoption Stage, Not Just Its Existence

**What it is** — Weber applies Rogers' innovation-adoption curve to performance technology: a tool's usefulness to a given department depends on where it sits on the maturity curve (early/skeptical adopters through mainstream use), not just on whether it exists or is popular elsewhere. His example: GPS moved from being met with skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: the curve "helps us understand how technology will be adopted and utilised within our environment", and staff knowledge and behaviour set how far up it a department can go (Webinar 1 Part II transcript 00:07:08 to 00:07:35). **Inference:** adopting before procedures and staff skill have matured likely recreates the tech-rich, procedure-poor problem (Lab_1c PDF p.1), the tool exists, but the surrounding discipline needed to use it well does not yet exist; see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]].

**When to apply** — Weighing a genuinely new technology (a novel wearable, an AI-based analysis tool) against an established one with known error, interpretation norms, and staff familiarity. The question this framework poses is not whether the tool is valid in principle, but whether the tool, and the staff's ability to use it, have matured to the point where adopting it now is worth the transition cost.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for placing a specific tool on the curve, and the maturity claim here is his own retrospective narrative about GPS, not a measured or validated adoption metric for any other technology. It should not be read as an argument to always wait for mainstream adoption. **Inference:** earlier-stage tools can still be worth adopting deliberately, with the added discipline that comes with being an early user.

**Example** — Weber's GPS timeline, per the lesson summary: he contrasts early adopters of new tools with GPS specifically, which he says moved from skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35). This is his personal recollection, not a documented industry history in this corpus. His other illustration is his own product, SpeedSig, placed at the innovator stage (00:05:16 to 00:05:45); an interested party's example.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit that reveals whether a department's procedures have caught up to a tool it already owns.

# Stoplight Storytelling

**What it is** — A short, repeatable presentation format for bringing a decision to a group: state the question or headline first (rather than opening with data that has no stated purpose); show status using green (go), amber (hold/monitor), or red (stop/change); present at most one chart, readable immediately, that addresses whether an observed difference is meaningful relative to measurement error, normal variation, and other convergent evidence; and close with a requested direction (start/stop/change) plus one owner, one action, a due date, and a review point recorded in the decision log (Lab 3C summary, 00:00–04:25; see [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]). Presentation rules: keep the message short, label axes and differences clearly, avoid dual axes and complex charts that require extended explanation, never bring multiple charts, multiple requests, or brand-new information into the moment, and give every status, including amber, a next action or review date (04:25–06:23). A roughly two-minute presentation is Weber's own benchmark, though he notes novel or complex issues may need pre-reading or a separate meeting instead (06:23–06:43). Timing is given two ways: about two minutes per slide (3C transcript 00:06:23 to 00:06:28; template p.2; cheat sheet p.2 "2 min per slide") and about five minutes per person, five presentations in 30 minutes (00:07:30 to 00:07:38).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated purpose, per the lesson summary, is to keep a sequence of presentations in one meeting from expanding into long, unfocused discussions, and to let staff present more autonomously once the shared format is understood (06:56–07:54). **Inference:** forcing one chart and one request likely removes the two most common ways a presentation drifts, adding more evidence than the room can process in the time available, and leaving the ask implicit so no decision actually gets made.

**When to apply** — Any recurring review where multiple practitioners each need to bring a status update that may require a decision: a weekly return-to-play review, a load-monitoring standup, or a technology-adoption check-in. Pairs directly with the kaigi format's evidence-precision rule (see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]) as the visual layer of the same discipline.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's two-minute benchmark and single-chart rule are explicitly not meant for novel or complex issues, which he says may need pre-reading or a dedicated meeting instead (06:23–06:43); **Inference:** forcing a genuinely complex, multi-variable problem into stoplight format would risk the same false simplicity the framework is otherwise designed to avoid (see [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]]). The timing and efficiency claims are Weber's own practice examples, not validated thresholds.

**Example** — The course's slide template (Lab_3c_Stoplight_Storytelling_Slide_Template.pdf p.1 to p.2): headline decision question; one stoplight status with a one-line reason; one chart with baseline, current, change, SEM and MDC95; at most two pieces of convergent evidence; one ask written as a verb (Start/Stop/Change/Limit/Continue); owner, action, due, review; footer "2 minutes total. If it needs explaining, it's the wrong meeting type."

# Strategy Is the Highway, Tactics Are Changing Lanes

**What it is** — Weber's delegation model: **strategy** is the department's direction, standards, and the key questions it cares about, described as "the highway"; **tactics** are the day-to-day choices staff make within that direction (which tool to deploy, how to adjust tests, timing, and exposure, how to respond to what they see), described as "changing lanes" (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1–2). The stated goal is to give staff tactical freedom while the leader maintains strategic alignment (p.2). He restates the same model in Webinar 3 Part III as a direct delegation rule: the leader names the destination and boundaries, staff choose tactics within them, with more discretion given to an experienced colleague than a new hire, and explicit criteria for which decisions must be escalated (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 03:56–06:30).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated goal is that the model gives staff tactical freedom while the leader maintains strategic alignment (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.2). Weber's stated mechanism: clear intent lets staff know "what can I make a decision on and what do I need to push up the chain", and staff without direction "become disillusioned. Their behavior will change", while micromanagement costs the leader control of time (Webinar 3 Part III transcript 00:05:18 to 00:06:30).

**When to apply** — Structuring how much autonomy a staff member has over test selection, session adjustments, or reporting choices, especially as a department scales past a size where informal alignment happens naturally. **Eric's baseline:** the Playbook's stated peer-department framing for Applied Performance ("enabling" other departments to answer their own questions) is not fully reconciled with a support-staff framing that also appears in the same corpus ("helping program and plan the training") [method-baseline.md Tensions #2]. **Inference:** naming the specific highway (standards, questions Applied Performance owns) versus the lanes (tactical choices left to individual practitioners) is a direct way to resolve that ambiguity in practice.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no method for determining where the highway's boundaries should sit for a given department or decision type; that judgment call is left entirely to the leader. It is also not a substitute for the formal escalation criteria a decision gate provides (see [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]) when the stakes are high enough to need a documented pass/fail/borderline threshold rather than a general delegation boundary.

**Example** — A first-year graduate gets "one or two lanes max"; a 10-year colleague gets "the full six lane highway" (Webinar 3 Part III transcript 00:04:38 to 00:04:51; Lab_3D blog p.1: "six-lane highway ... but nobody drives off-road").

# The Tech Stack Reality Check

**What it is** — A three-step audit for an existing department, done before buying anything new. Step 1: inventory what you have **as measurement systems, not brands** ("people say 'we're doing NordBord.' NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength," Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). Weber's named categories: your computer (spreadsheets vs. real analysis/dashboard/coding capability), wearables (GNSS/GPS + IMU, not just "GPS"), force plates (force over time, not "jump height machines"), force transducers/load cells (isometrics, Nordics, dynamometry, where "if your setup changes, your test changes"), and linear position transducers (GymAware/FLEX-style, which need standardized naming, setup, ROM rules, and reporting rules) (pp.1–3). Step 2: for each measurement, establish **reliability** — can you repeat the number within a known error band, both within-session and between-session (p.3; Lab 1C transcript 00:03:47–00:04:45). Step 3: write down the **procedure** (warm-up, familiarization, instructions, trial structure) for at least one tool, because "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures... a procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:04:45–00:05:02; PDF p.3).

**Why it works** — Weber's argument is that many performance environments are "tech-rich and procedure-poor" (PDF p.1), which produces noise and decisions that feel like guesswork. Confusing a brand for the underlying test hides what is actually being measured; skipping reliability means a department will, in his words, "chase noise and call it insight" (PDF p.3) the first time two measurements disagree.

**When to apply** — Before adding new technology, and as a standing onboarding document for new staff ("if you started a job this week... you need to be able to set standards for your staff to follow," Lab 1C transcript 00:05:07–00:05:29). **Eric's baseline:** documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting), except for the Catapult workflow, which has genuine operational depth [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2]. **Inference:** this audit's Step 1-3 sequence is a concrete way to close that gap tool by tool.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a starting-point audit, not a statistics course; it names ICC/typical-error-style reliability concepts only in passing (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the fuller treatment). It also assumes a department already owns the technology being audited; it is not a tool-selection or purchasing framework, and it takes no position on which tools are worth owning in the first place.

**Example** — Weber's own admission that most practitioners "treat their laptop like a typewriter" (Lab_1c PDF p.1) and his contrast with himself ("Now that's me because I want to know and I want to be able to push myself further up the chain") illustrates the audit's first, most-overlooked category: the computer itself as a performance tool (Lab 1C transcript 00:01:13–00:02:32; see [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]] — the specific claim about computer/coding skill this audit surfaces. [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]] — the companion audit that adds who-does-what-with-it. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistics behind Step 2. [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the chain this audit sets up (procedure to reliability to confidence to defensible decisions).

# The Tech Stack Reality Check

**What it is** — A three-step audit for an existing department, done before buying anything new. Step 1: inventory what you have **as measurement systems, not brands** ("people say 'we're doing NordBord.' NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength," Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). Weber's named categories: your computer (spreadsheets vs. real analysis/dashboard/coding capability), wearables (GNSS/GPS + IMU, not just "GPS"), force plates (force over time, not "jump height machines"), force transducers/load cells (isometrics, Nordics, dynamometry, where "if your setup changes, your test changes"), and linear position transducers (GymAware/FLEX-style, which need standardized naming, setup, ROM rules, and reporting rules) (pp.1–3). Step 2: for each measurement, establish **reliability**: can you repeat the number within a known error band, both within-session and between-session (p.3; Lab 1C transcript 00:03:47–00:04:45). Step 3: write down the **procedure** (warm-up, familiarization, instructions, trial structure) for at least one tool, because "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures... a procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:04:45–00:05:02; PDF p.3).

**Why it works** — Weber's argument is that many performance environments are "tech-rich and procedure-poor" (PDF p.1), which produces noise and decisions that feel like guesswork. Confusing a brand for the underlying test hides what is actually being measured; skipping reliability means a department will, in his words, "chase noise and call it insight" (PDF p.3) the first time two measurements disagree.

**When to apply** — Before adding new technology, and as a standing onboarding document for new staff ("if you started a job this week... you need to be able to set standards for your staff to follow," Lab 1C transcript 00:05:07–00:05:29). **Eric's baseline:** documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting), except for the Catapult workflow, which has genuine operational depth [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2]. **Inference:** this audit's Step 1-3 sequence is a concrete way to close that gap tool by tool.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a starting-point audit, not a statistics course; it names ICC/typical-error-style reliability concepts only in passing (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the fuller treatment). It also assumes a department already owns the technology being audited; it is not a tool-selection or purchasing framework, and it takes no position on which tools are worth owning in the first place.

**Example** — Weber's own admission that most practitioners "treat their laptop like a typewriter" (Lab_1c PDF p.1) and his contrast with himself ("Now that's me because I want to know and I want to be able to push myself further up the chain") illustrates the audit's first, most-overlooked category: the computer itself as a performance tool (Lab 1C transcript 00:01:13–00:02:32; see [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]]).

13	
14	# Give Staff Ownership of a Meeting to Build Their Leadership Skill
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber treats running a meeting as a deliberate developmental exercise: giving a staff member ownership of a meeting's structure, concise communication, follow-up, and accountability builds confidence and practical leadership skill (Lab 3D summary, 00:46–02:25). His own example: assigning a medical review meeting to his head physiotherapist. The head-physio example (00:02:05 to 00:02:20) is Weber's own account, untested. Implementation notes: define the meeting's purpose, keep an agenda, hold time limits and agreed decision boundaries, and record an owner/action/due-date/review for each output, while giving the facilitator room to make tactical choices within the larger strategy (02:25–03:11; see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]]). For less confident speakers, start small: one slide, one topic, a short time slot, then increase responsibility over time, and deliberately track who contributes so quieter staff are invited in with advance notice of when they will present (03:11–05:09).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's own described practice is graduated exposure: start with a small meeting, one slide, one topic, a short time slot, then increase responsibility over time (Lab 3D summary, 03:11–05:09). Weber's stated reasons: it teaches structure, concise communication, decision and follow-up habits, and builds confidence and trust; it also moves follow-up work off the leader (3D transcript 00:00:51 to 00:01:52). **Inference:** this likely works because a staff member given a bounded, low-stakes facilitation role practices the mechanics of running structured discussion without the full weight of an open-ended meeting, then earns larger scope as competence shows. This mirrors the knowledge x behaviour matrix's developmental use (see [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]): meeting ownership is a concrete vehicle for moving someone along the knowledge axis.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Identifying a staff member or intern ready for more responsibility, or building a structured on-ramp for a quieter staff member who has relevant expertise but does not volunteer it. **Eric's baseline:** the proposed intern curriculum's stated design principle is that interns should leave with "a professional portfolio of real work products (dashboards, reports, presentations, infographics)," not just device-operation checklists [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.4]. **Inference:** running an assigned meeting segment, with the agenda and decision log as artifacts, is one such work product.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — The course gives a readiness rule but leaves the bar blank: pick 3 to 5 observable behaviours (meeting type named, time boxes kept, asks written as verbs, outputs captured, ended on time) and step up only when the person hits a set number of them over a four-rep ladder (Lab_3D_Worksheet p.1 to p.2). **Inference:** this heuristic also assumes the leader is willing to accept the facilitation being less polished at first than if the leader ran it themselves; it is a deliberate trade of short-term efficiency for staff development.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's advancement path: start with a small meeting, one slide, one topic, a short time slot; increase responsibility from there (03:11–05:09).
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the broader developmental framework this practice serves. [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]] — the companion senior-leadership practice from the same lab.
27

13	
14	# Choose a Mentor Above You Who Has Worked in Elite Sport
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's rule: a mentor should sit above you on the knowledge axis (practitioner or operator) and have worked at the level you aim for (Olympic, NFL, EPL, AFL); your main mentor cannot be someone who has never worked in sport (Lab 1B Part 1 transcript 00:06:10 to 00:07:07; Lab_1b PDF p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated reason: elite sport's "the accountability process, the detail, the timing, the tempo" cannot be learned from someone who has not worked in it (00:07:07 to 00:07:13).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Assigning a mentor to a new hire, intern, or staff member being developed toward more responsibility, when there is a real choice between a mentor who has worked in elite sport and one who has not. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's proposed intern curriculum is explicitly adapting a Clemson Olympic-sports model "to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5]. Inference: for Baylor interns, the mentor pool should include staff who have worked at the level the intern is aiming for.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — This is Weber's stated opinion, not a tested claim; he gives no comparison of outcomes between mentors who have worked in elite sport and those who have not, and no guidance for cases where no such mentor is available above you. In that case the choice is between an imperfect option and no mentor at all, which this heuristic does not address.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's framing places this immediately after his call for aspiring leaders to start practicing leadership before they hold the title (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 02:36–03:59), positioning mentor selection as part of a deliberate leadership-development pipeline rather than an incidental pairing.
25	
26	**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] — the companion practice for identifying who needs a mentor. [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the grid this selection criterion sits inside.

14	# Your Computer Is Probably Your Most Underused Piece of Performance Technology
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's claim, made twice in the course (Lab 1C transcript and PDF), that the laptop most practitioners already own is, in Weber's words, "the most powerful piece of performance tech you own", yet "most people use computers like their typewriter" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:01:13–00:01:29; Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). He frames the gap as capability, not access: what a staff member can build, automate, analyze, visualize, and report determines what the rest of the tech stack is worth. His own example, per the transcript (which renders "strength and conditioning" as "straight conditioning," an evident ASR error): "I've been a [strength and] conditioning coach for over 30 years, but I can code fluently, I can run machine learning models, I can build AI tools within my system, I can build websites" (00:01:46–00:02:05).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's own stated rationale ties directly to his data-information-knowledge-wisdom hierarchy (see [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]]): "you can't do that without using your computer and advanced computer skills" (00:02:09–00:02:20). **Inference:** a department can own every wearable and force plate on the market and still be unable to turn the resulting exports into an interpretable report if no one on staff can code or build a dashboard.
19	
20	**When to apply** — When auditing staff capability alongside equipment (Lab 2B's capability-and-workflow audit; see [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]]), or when deciding where professional-development time should go before the next equipment purchase. **Eric's baseline:** Eric's own gap analysis names sport-specific data dictionaries and Baylor-specific technology workflows as unfinished, prioritized work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3]. **Inference:** that work depends on exactly this computer/coding capability existing on staff, not just on the vendor tools themselves.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber is careful to say "you don't need to become a programmer" (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1); this is not a claim that every S&C coach must learn to code. Inference: the department's analytic ceiling is set by whoever's computer skill is highest. It also doesn't specify which skills matter most (spreadsheets vs. dashboards vs. scripting) or how to build them; it names the gap, not the curriculum.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own audit question set for this category: what computer do you actually have, what do you use beyond spreadsheets, and can you run data workflows or dashboards when needed (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1).
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this claim is drawn from. [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]] — why computer skill is the bottleneck between data and decisions.
27

# Schedule Time to Ask What Could Break the System, Before It Does

**What it is** — Weber's closing recommendation in Podcast 6: leaders should set aside regular time outside daily operations specifically to ask what could derail a plan or expose a weakness in the department's system, rather than waiting for a failure to force the review (Podcast 6 summary, 00:00–01:41, 11:13–13:58). His stated reasoning: a team can share a common process and still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure (03:22–04:06) — the same blind spot his structured-dissent practices (see [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]]) are meant to catch inside a specific meeting, applied here as a standing habit rather than a one-off intervention.

**Why it works** — **Inference:** a system that is currently working provides no natural trigger to question it; problems tend to surface only after something has already gone wrong. Scheduling the review removes the dependency on a failure event, and revising the system as staff, technology, and knowledge change treats department process as something that ages and needs periodic maintenance, not a one-time setup. Weber's stated reason: people, technology and information change, so a working system drifts, and "what seems nice and stable ... may unravel at the point when you don't need it to" (Podcast 6 transcript 00:12:12 to 00:13:36).

**When to apply** — At a natural cadence point (end of season, start of a new training block, after staff turnover, or when a new technology is adopted), independent of whether anything has visibly gone wrong. **Eric's baseline:** a three-phase roadmap ends with an annual Playbook review cycle each May [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]. **Inference:** this heuristic argues that review should explicitly include the question of what could break the system, not only an update-the-document pass.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own illustration (a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team that only changed course once a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept) is a personal anecdote about decision dynamics; the transcript does not establish the injuries' actual cause or the training change's effect, and should not be read as evidence for a specific calf-injury intervention (Podcast 6 summary, 08:04–10:00). This heuristic also gives no specific cadence or format for the review — only that it should happen on a schedule rather than only reactively.

**Example** — Weber's own framing of the practice: identify what could go wrong in an apparently stable system, and revise it as staff, technology, and knowledge change (11:13–13:58).

**Related** — [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]] — the in-meeting version of the same challenge-your-own-plan discipline. [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the broader case for documented, periodically reviewed procedure.

# Give Staff Ownership of a Meeting to Build Their Leadership Skill

**What it is** — Weber treats running a meeting as a deliberate developmental exercise: giving a staff member ownership of a meeting's structure, concise communication, follow-up, and accountability builds confidence and practical leadership skill (Lab 3D summary, 00:46–02:25). His own example: assigning a medical review meeting to his head physiotherapist. The head-physio example (00:02:05 to 00:02:20) is Weber's own account, untested. Implementation notes: define the meeting's purpose, keep an agenda, hold time limits and agreed decision boundaries, and record an owner/action/due-date/review for each output, while giving the facilitator room to make tactical choices within the larger strategy (02:25–03:11; see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]]). For less confident speakers, start small: one slide, one topic, a short time slot, then increase responsibility over time, and deliberately track who contributes so quieter staff are invited in with advance notice of when they will present (03:11–05:09).

**Why it works** — Weber's own described practice is graduated exposure: start with a small meeting, one slide, one topic, a short time slot, then increase responsibility over time (Lab 3D summary, 03:11–05:09). Weber's stated reasons: it teaches structure, concise communication, decision and follow-up habits, and builds confidence and trust; it also moves follow-up work off the leader (3D transcript 00:00:51 to 00:01:52). **Inference:** this likely works because a staff member given a bounded, low-stakes facilitation role practices the mechanics of running structured discussion without the full weight of an open-ended meeting, then earns larger scope as competence shows. This mirrors the knowledge x behaviour matrix's developmental use (see [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]): meeting ownership is a concrete vehicle for moving someone along the knowledge axis.

**When to apply** — Identifying a staff member or intern ready for more responsibility, or building a structured on-ramp for a quieter staff member who has relevant expertise but does not volunteer it. **Eric's baseline:** the proposed intern curriculum's stated design principle is that interns should leave with "a professional portfolio of real work products (dashboards, reports, presentations, infographics)," not just device-operation checklists [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.4]. **Inference:** running an assigned meeting segment, with the agenda and decision log as artifacts, is one such work product.

**When NOT to apply** — The course gives a readiness rule but leaves the bar blank: pick 3 to 5 observable behaviours (meeting type named, time boxes kept, asks written as verbs, outputs captured, ended on time) and step up only when the person hits a set number of them over a four-rep ladder (Lab_3D_Worksheet p.1 to p.2). **Inference:** this heuristic also assumes the leader is willing to accept the facilitation being less polished at first than if the leader ran it themselves; it is a deliberate trade of short-term efficiency for staff development.

**Example** — Weber's advancement path: start with a small meeting, one slide, one topic, a short time slot; increase responsibility from there (03:11–05:09).

**Related** — [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the broader developmental framework this practice serves. [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]] — the companion senior-leadership practice from the same lab.

# Choose a Mentor Above You Who Has Worked in Elite Sport

**What it is** — Weber's rule: a mentor should sit above you on the knowledge axis (practitioner or operator) and have worked at the level you aim for (Olympic, NFL, EPL, AFL); your main mentor cannot be someone who has never worked in sport (Lab 1B Part 1 transcript 00:06:10 to 00:07:07; Lab_1b PDF p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated reason: elite sport's "the accountability process, the detail, the timing, the tempo" cannot be learned from someone who has not worked in it (00:07:07 to 00:07:13).

**When to apply** — Assigning a mentor to a new hire, intern, or staff member being developed toward more responsibility, when there is a real choice between a mentor who has worked in elite sport and one who has not. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's proposed intern curriculum is explicitly adapting a Clemson Olympic-sports model "to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5]. Inference: for Baylor interns, the mentor pool should include staff who have worked at the level the intern is aiming for.

**When NOT to apply** — This is Weber's stated opinion, not a tested claim; he gives no comparison of outcomes between mentors who have worked in elite sport and those who have not, and no guidance for cases where no such mentor is available above you. In that case the choice is between an imperfect option and no mentor at all, which this heuristic does not address.

**Example** — Weber's framing places this immediately after his call for aspiring leaders to start practicing leadership before they hold the title (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 02:36–03:59), positioning mentor selection as part of a deliberate leadership-development pipeline rather than an incidental pairing.

**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] — the companion practice for identifying who needs a mentor. [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the grid this selection criterion sits inside.

# Your Computer Is Probably Your Most Underused Piece of Performance Technology

**What it is** — Weber's claim, made twice in the course (Lab 1C transcript and PDF), that the laptop most practitioners already own is, in Weber's words, "the most powerful piece of performance tech you own", yet "most people use computers like their typewriter" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:01:13–00:01:29; Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). He frames the gap as capability, not access: what a staff member can build, automate, analyze, visualize, and report determines what the rest of the tech stack is worth. His own example, per the transcript (which renders "strength and conditioning" as "straight conditioning," an evident ASR error): "I've been a [strength and] conditioning coach for over 30 years, but I can code fluently, I can run machine learning models, I can build AI tools within my system, I can build websites" (00:01:46–00:02:05).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated rationale ties directly to his data-information-knowledge-wisdom hierarchy (see [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]]): "you can't do that without using your computer and advanced computer skills" (00:02:09–00:02:20). **Inference:** a department can own every wearable and force plate on the market and still be unable to turn the resulting exports into an interpretable report if no one on staff can code or build a dashboard.

**When to apply** — When auditing staff capability alongside equipment (Lab 2B's capability-and-workflow audit; see [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]]), or when deciding where professional-development time should go before the next equipment purchase. **Eric's baseline:** Eric's own gap analysis names sport-specific data dictionaries and Baylor-specific technology workflows as unfinished, prioritized work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3]. **Inference:** that work depends on exactly this computer/coding capability existing on staff, not just on the vendor tools themselves.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is careful to say "you don't need to become a programmer" (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1); this is not a claim that every S&C coach must learn to code. Inference: the department's analytic ceiling is set by whoever's computer skill is highest. It also doesn't specify which skills matter most (spreadsheets vs. dashboards vs. scripting) or how to build them; it names the gap, not the curriculum.

**Example** — Weber's own audit question set for this category: what computer do you actually have, what do you use beyond spreadsheets, and can you run data workflows or dashboards when needed (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1).

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this claim is drawn from. [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]] — why computer skill is the bottleneck between data and decisions.
