# Ask Staff About Their CPD to Surface Both Support Needs and Ambition

**What it is** — Weber's suggested practice: ask staff directly about their continuing professional development (CPD) and invite brief presentations about something they recently learned (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21). He pairs this with a related opening exercise, from a colleague's 60-second exercise for a leadership group: write down the five things that could stop this from working (00:01:26 to 00:01:45), as a way to get people examining their own contribution and the team's bottlenecks.

**Why it works** — Weber's stated reason: asking staff to present "starts to show you where they're at", and he uses it as a check on staff who may be handbrakes (Lab 1B Part 1 transcript 00:04:04 to 00:04:58). **Inference:** the same conversation can also separate a knowledge gap from a motivation gap, which maps onto the knowledge x behaviour matrix's two axes (see [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]).

**When to apply** — Regular staff check-ins, annual development conversations, or when trying to figure out who on staff is ready for more responsibility versus who needs a defined training plan. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's proposed intern curriculum already states interns should leave with "a professional portfolio of real work products," not just device-operation checklists [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.4]. **Inference:** a CPD check-in is a low-cost way to track whether that portfolio is actually forming.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no structure for how often to ask, what to do with the answer, or how to handle a staff member who cannot name any recent CPD; this is a prompt, not a full performance-management process. It also should not be the sole input into a personnel decision (see the caution in [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]).

**Example** — Weber's own framing, per the lesson summary: asking staff about CPD and inviting a short presentation on something recently learned, as a low-friction way to open the conversation (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21).

# Schedule Time to Ask What Could Break the System, Before It Does

**What it is** — Weber's closing recommendation in Podcast 6: leaders should set aside regular time outside daily operations specifically to ask what could derail a plan or expose a weakness in the department's system, rather than waiting for a failure to force the review (Podcast 6 summary, 00:00–01:41, 11:13–13:58). His stated reasoning: a team can share a common process and still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure (03:22–04:06) — the same blind spot his structured-dissent practices (see [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]]) are meant to catch inside a specific meeting, applied here as a standing habit rather than a one-off intervention.

**Why it works** — **Inference:** a system that is currently working provides no natural trigger to question it; problems tend to surface only after something has already gone wrong. Scheduling the review removes the dependency on a failure event, and revising the system as staff, technology, and knowledge change treats department process as something that ages and needs periodic maintenance, not a one-time setup. Weber's stated reason: people, technology and information change, so a working system drifts, and "what seems nice and stable ... may unravel at the point when you don't need it to" (Podcast 6 transcript 00:12:12 to 00:13:36).

**When to apply** — At a natural cadence point (end of season, start of a new training block, after staff turnover, or when a new technology is adopted), independent of whether anything has visibly gone wrong. **Eric's baseline:** a three-phase roadmap ends with an annual Playbook review cycle each May [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]. **Inference:** this heuristic argues that review should explicitly include the question of what could break the system, not only an update-the-document pass.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own illustration (a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team that only changed course once a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept) is a personal anecdote about decision dynamics; the transcript does not establish the injuries' actual cause or the training change's effect, and should not be read as evidence for a specific calf-injury intervention (Podcast 6 summary, 08:04–10:00). This heuristic also gives no specific cadence or format for the review — only that it should happen on a schedule rather than only reactively.

**Example** — Weber's own framing of the practice: identify what could go wrong in an apparently stable system, and revise it as staff, technology, and knowledge change (11:13–13:58).

**Related** — [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]] — the in-meeting version of the same challenge-your-own-plan discipline. [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the broader case for documented, periodically reviewed procedure.

14	# Rolling Averages Answer "Drifting This Week?", Not "Improved This Phase?"
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's specific caution inside the monitoring-vs-testing framework (see [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]]): rolling averages and exponentially weighted moving averages are excellent at answering "is the athlete drifting from baseline this week," but they are not designed to answer "did the athlete improve meaningfully across a training phase" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1–2). His fix: long-term change needs comparisons that respect time blocks and phase structure (pre vs. post, block vs. block), not continuous smoothing (p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — **Inference:** a rolling window is, by construction, always chasing the most recent values. If an athlete's true capacity drifts down gradually over a training block, a rolling average would likely track that drift and never flag it as a deviation, because the reference point itself has quietly moved with the athlete. The same window that makes short-term monitoring useful (fast reaction to recent change) is what makes it blind to slow change. Weber himself states the effect (rolling averages answer a different question than phase-level testing) without spelling out this mechanism.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any metric tracked with a rolling window or EWMA for daily/weekly monitoring that is also, informally or formally, being used to answer a phase-level question of whether the athlete's capacity actually improved. **Eric's baseline:** weekly tracking is stated as preferred over infrequent, once-a-phase testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment]. **Inference:** this heuristic is the specific mechanism behind the broader tension flagged in [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] between Weber's framework and that stated preference.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — This is not an argument against rolling averages for their intended purpose (short-term status and load-adjustment decisions); it is a warning against also treating the same rolling number as evidence of long-term program effectiveness. It also does not specify how wide a rolling window should be for a given metric, only that no window substitutes for a genuine pre/post or block/block comparison.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own instruction: to evaluate a training phase, compare defined phases or time points (pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two) rather than relying on the continuous smoothing used for weekly monitoring (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1).
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the parent framework this heuristic sits inside. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistics for deciding whether any observed change, rolling or block-based, is real.
27

14	# Agree Which Channel Carries What, and When, Before the Pressure Arrives
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's set of communication rules meant to be settled in advance rather than negotiated in the moment: specify which channel carries each kind of information and what behavior is expected on it; for injuries specifically, state in advance when the coach receives a provisional update and when a more specific medical update may follow; agree the timing and form of post-training reports, since different coaches want very different amounts and formats; mark messages by urgency or purpose; and make meeting invitations state their objective, length, and required preparation, with project assignments stating the deliverable, deadline, expected quality, and people to consult, plus expected response times (Webinar 3 Part II summary, 06:11–10:09). In Part III he adds three more standing practices from the same "discipline equals freedom" chain (see [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]]): document routine work so it is clear who handles equipment, session prep, data collection, and testing; remove avoidable ambiguity by stating a meeting's purpose, deadline, and each person's role; and schedule regular feedback check-ins, addressing performance issues promptly and asking staff for feedback on the leader's own leadership (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–09:15).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism ties directly to attention management: predictable communication and clear roles reduce the time a leader spends interpreting routine requests, freeing that attention for planning and harder problems (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 00:00–00:59, 02:52–05:05). His example: a head coach, doctor, and strength coach may all ask about training load from entirely different concerns and technical backgrounds, so the leader needs pre-agreed shared language and channel norms to respond efficiently rather than re-deriving the right answer for each asker every time (00:59–02:46).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Setting up communication norms for a new season, a new coach relationship, or a newly formed interdisciplinary group, particularly around injury updates, where ambiguity about timing is most costly. **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and Athletic Medicine's decisions [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** this heuristic is the channel-and-timing layer that makes that advisory information actually arrive when it is needed.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber's claims about cognitive effects and communication methods are presented as his own management practice, not independently validated outcomes (Webinar 3 Part II summary caveat). This is also not a substitute for the decision-gate timeframes in [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]], which cover the higher-stakes case of formal go/hold/stop decisions rather than routine reporting cadence. Inference: Weber's mechanism rests on a decision-fatigue or willpower-depletion account he does not source (Webinar 3 Part I transcript 00:02:52 to 00:03:17, 00:09:03 to 00:09:11); that literature is contested, so treat the time-saving rationale as his experience, not an established effect.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's military-analogy caution in Part I: he explicitly warns that military and sport stakes differ, using the analogy only to illustrate that rehearsed communication routines let a team act without inventing a process under pressure — in one AFL case, coach and performance staff adjusted a training session mid-session (dropping a drill, extending another, pulling named players on exposure) because they shared enough technical language to estimate consequences for specific players in real time (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 05:05–09:03). Untested anecdote, Weber's own account.
25

13	
14	# Assign Someone to Argue the Other Side Before You Decide
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber describes an International Rugby Union coach (and CEOs he has observed) who stated a problem, then sat silent until staff had spoken, so the leader's view did not bias the decision (3D transcript 00:06:25 to 00:07:08; Podcast 6 00:05:04 to 00:06:03; Lab_3D blog p.2: "pose the problem…then sit quietly"). His own practice is to assign one staff member to "argue the opposite. Find data, find anything to argue the opposite" (3D 00:07:24 to 00:07:37), the same idea behind the "tenth man" device from *World War Z* he also names (assign someone to formally argue against the group's favored explanation). He cites de Bono's six hats but says he has never used it in a meeting; his own version is to rule that "for the next five minutes, you can only speak data" (Podcast 6 00:06:34 to 00:07:25). He also describes a coach who listened quietly before asking specifically where a plan might fail (04:59–06:34).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's own stated reasoning, per the lesson summary, is that a team sharing one process can still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure (Podcast 6 summary, 00:00–01:41, 03:22–04:06). **Inference:** a leader who speaks first likely sets an anchor that makes dissent socially costly for everyone after them; formally assigning the dissenting role removes that social cost, since the person arguing against the plan is doing their job, not breaking rank.

# Assign Someone to Argue the Other Side Before You Decide

**What it is** — Weber describes an International Rugby Union coach (and CEOs he has observed) who stated a problem, then sat silent until staff had spoken, so the leader's view did not bias the decision (3D transcript 00:06:25 to 00:07:08; Podcast 6 00:05:04 to 00:06:03; Lab_3D blog p.2: "pose the problem…then sit quietly"). His own practice is to assign one staff member to "argue the opposite. Find data, find anything to argue the opposite" (3D 00:07:24 to 00:07:37), the same idea behind the "tenth man" device from *World War Z* he also names (assign someone to formally argue against the group's favored explanation). He cites de Bono's six hats but says he has never used it in a meeting; his own version is to rule that "for the next five minutes, you can only speak data" (Podcast 6 00:06:34 to 00:07:25). He also describes a coach who listened quietly before asking specifically where a plan might fail (04:59–06:34).

# Rolling Averages Answer "Drifting This Week?", Not "Improved This Phase?"

**What it is** — Weber's specific caution inside the monitoring-vs-testing framework (see [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]]): rolling averages and exponentially weighted moving averages are excellent at answering "is the athlete drifting from baseline this week," but they are not designed to answer "did the athlete improve meaningfully across a training phase" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1–2). His fix: long-term change needs comparisons that respect time blocks and phase structure (pre vs. post, block vs. block), not continuous smoothing (p.2).

**Why it works** — **Inference:** a rolling window is, by construction, always chasing the most recent values. If an athlete's true capacity drifts down gradually over a training block, a rolling average would likely track that drift and never flag it as a deviation, because the reference point itself has quietly moved with the athlete. The same window that makes short-term monitoring useful (fast reaction to recent change) is what makes it blind to slow change. Weber himself states the effect (rolling averages answer a different question than phase-level testing) without spelling out this mechanism.

**When to apply** — Any metric tracked with a rolling window or EWMA for daily/weekly monitoring that is also, informally or formally, being used to answer a phase-level question of whether the athlete's capacity actually improved. **Eric's baseline:** weekly tracking is stated as preferred over infrequent, once-a-phase testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment]. **Inference:** this heuristic is the specific mechanism behind the broader tension flagged in [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] between Weber's framework and that stated preference.

**When NOT to apply** — This is not an argument against rolling averages for their intended purpose (short-term status and load-adjustment decisions); it is a warning against also treating the same rolling number as evidence of long-term program effectiveness. It also does not specify how wide a rolling window should be for a given metric, only that no window substitutes for a genuine pre/post or block/block comparison.

**Example** — Weber's own instruction: to evaluate a training phase, compare defined phases or time points (pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two) rather than relying on the continuous smoothing used for weekly monitoring (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1).

# Agree Which Channel Carries What, and When, Before the Pressure Arrives

**What it is** — Weber's set of communication rules meant to be settled in advance rather than negotiated in the moment: specify which channel carries each kind of information and what behavior is expected on it; for injuries specifically, state in advance when the coach receives a provisional update and when a more specific medical update may follow; agree the timing and form of post-training reports, since different coaches want very different amounts and formats; mark messages by urgency or purpose; and make meeting invitations state their objective, length, and required preparation, with project assignments stating the deliverable, deadline, expected quality, and people to consult, plus expected response times (Webinar 3 Part II summary, 06:11–10:09). In Part III he adds three more standing practices from the same "discipline equals freedom" chain (see [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]]): document routine work so it is clear who handles equipment, session prep, data collection, and testing; remove avoidable ambiguity by stating a meeting's purpose, deadline, and each person's role; and schedule regular feedback check-ins, addressing performance issues promptly and asking staff for feedback on the leader's own leadership (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–09:15).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism ties directly to attention management: predictable communication and clear roles reduce the time a leader spends interpreting routine requests, freeing that attention for planning and harder problems (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 00:00–00:59, 02:52–05:05). His example: a head coach, doctor, and strength coach may all ask about training load from entirely different concerns and technical backgrounds, so the leader needs pre-agreed shared language and channel norms to respond efficiently rather than re-deriving the right answer for each asker every time (00:59–02:46).

**When to apply** — Setting up communication norms for a new season, a new coach relationship, or a newly formed interdisciplinary group, particularly around injury updates, where ambiguity about timing is most costly. **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and Athletic Medicine's decisions [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** this heuristic is the channel-and-timing layer that makes that advisory information actually arrive when it is needed.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's claims about cognitive effects and communication methods are presented as his own management practice, not independently validated outcomes (Webinar 3 Part II summary caveat). This is also not a substitute for the decision-gate timeframes in [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]], which cover the higher-stakes case of formal go/hold/stop decisions rather than routine reporting cadence. Inference: Weber's mechanism rests on a decision-fatigue or willpower-depletion account he does not source (Webinar 3 Part I transcript 00:02:52 to 00:03:17, 00:09:03 to 00:09:11); that literature is contested, so treat the time-saving rationale as his experience, not an established effect.

**Example** — Weber's military-analogy caution in Part I: he explicitly warns that military and sport stakes differ, using the analogy only to illustrate that rehearsed communication routines let a team act without inventing a process under pressure — in one AFL case, coach and performance staff adjusted a training session mid-session (dropping a drill, extending another, pulling named players on exposure) because they shared enough technical language to estimate consequences for specific players in real time (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 05:05–09:03). Untested anecdote, Weber's own account.

**Related** — [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the underlying chain this set of rules extends. **Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism ties directly to attention management: predictable communication and clear roles reduce the time a leader spends interpreting routine requests, freeing that attention for planning and harder problems (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 00:00–00:59, 02:52–05:05). His example: a head coach, doctor, and strength coach may all ask about training load from entirely different concerns and technical backgrounds, so the leader needs pre-agreed shared language and channel norms to respond efficiently rather than re-deriving the right answer for each asker every time (00:59–02:46).

**When to apply** — Setting up communication norms for a new season, a new coach relationship, or a newly formed interdisciplinary group, particularly around injury updates, where ambiguity about timing is most costly. **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and Athletic Medicine's decisions [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** this heuristic is the channel-and-timing layer that makes that advisory information actually arrive when it is needed.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's claims about cognitive effects and communication methods are presented as his own management practice, not independently validated outcomes (Webinar 3 Part II summary caveat). This is also not a substitute for the decision-gate timeframes in [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]], which cover the higher-stakes case of formal go/hold/stop decisions rather than routine reporting cadence. Inference: Weber's mechanism rests on a decision-fatigue or willpower-depletion account he does not source (Webinar 3 Part I transcript 00:02:52 to 00:03:17, 00:09:03 to 00:09:11); that literature is contested, so treat the time-saving rationale as his experience, not an established effect.

# Assign Someone to Argue the Other Side Before You Decide

**What it is** — Weber describes an International Rugby Union coach (and CEOs he has observed) who stated a problem, then sat silent until staff had spoken, so the leader's view did not bias the decision (3D transcript 00:06:25 to 00:07:08; Podcast 6 00:05:04 to 00:06:03; Lab_3D blog p.2: "pose the problem…then sit quietly"). His own practice is to assign one staff member to "argue the opposite. Find data, find anything to argue the opposite" (3D 00:07:24 to 00:07:37), the same idea behind the "tenth man" device from *World War Z* he also names (assign someone to formally argue against the group's favored explanation). He cites de Bono's six hats but says he has never used it in a meeting; his own version is to rule that "for the next five minutes, you can only speak data" (Podcast 6 00:06:34 to 00:07:25). He also describes a coach who listened quietly before asking specifically where a plan might fail (04:59–06:34).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated reasoning, per the lesson summary, is that a team sharing one process can still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure (Podcast 6 summary, 00:00–01:41, 03:22–04:06). **Inference:** a leader who speaks first likely sets an anchor that makes dissent socially costly for everyone after them; formally assigning the dissenting role removes that social cost, since the person arguing against the plan is doing their job, not breaking rank.

**When to apply** — High-stakes or hard-to-reverse decisions, especially ones the group has converged on quickly or that fit a familiar pattern the department has not recently questioned. Weber's own recurring calf-injury anecdote (a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team that only changed course once a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept) is his illustration of what happens when dissent has no formal channel and instead depends on finding the right messenger after the fact (Podcast 6 summary, 08:04–10:00).

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for which decisions warrant an assigned dissenter versus ordinary discussion. **Inference:** using it for every routine call would likely slow decision-making without adding much value. The film and historical references (World War Z, six hats) are illustrations of the practice, not evidence for its effectiveness in a performance department, and the calf-injury anecdote is a personal account that does not establish the training change's actual effect on injury rates.

**Example** — Weber's own account, per the lesson summary: a coach who listened quietly before asking specifically where a plan might fail, rather than stating a view first and then asking for objections to it (04:59–06:34).

# Report in the Coach's Existing Words, Without Losing the Link to the Measurement

**What it is** — Weber's recommendation: replace technical language with terms the audience already uses, while keeping the connection back to the underlying measurement intact. His AFL example: he and a coach agreed on verbal running categories, then used those categories in reporting rather than leading with speed units (Webinar 3 Part II summary, 01:09–06:11). He recommends explaining processes in plain terms, documenting them where useful, offering coaches short reference sheets, and learning a given coach's preferred words and report format early in the season, since different coaches want very different amounts and formats of information (07:48–08:39).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: without a common language "communication becomes translation", with a high "mental cost" (Webinar 3 Part II transcript 00:01:09 to 00:01:50), and a coach who hears their own words back gains confidence in the report (00:05:55 to 00:06:00). He sources the second point to neuro-linguistic programming (00:05:40), which has little empirical support; treat it as his experience. **Inference:** agreeing verbal categories once removes the translation step from every later report, the same recipient-question discipline as [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] and the failure mode named in [[heuristic--replace-translation-with-early-education]].

**When to apply** — Building or revising any coach-facing report template, and specifically at the start of a season or with a new coach, before habits and expectations have set. **Eric's baseline:** standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2]. **Inference:** this heuristic argues the template design process should start with the coach's own vocabulary, established early, rather than a generic vendor-report format.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber does not argue for dropping technical precision internally among performance and medical staff, only for translating it at the coach-facing layer; the underlying measurement and its documented reliability (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) should not be diluted, only re-expressed. It also assumes a coach's preferred vocabulary is knowable and stable enough to build a template around. **Inference:** for a new coach, that may take a full season to establish.

**Example** — Weber's specific practice: verbal running categories, agreed once with the coach ("jog, stride, sprint, gut run", 00:02:37 to 00:03:22), used consistently in reporting instead of raw speed-band units (01:09–06:11).

**Related** — [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — the general communication principle this applies to coaches specifically. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]] — the companion rules for when and how coach-facing information is delivered.

14	# Discipline Equals Freedom: Procedure, Not the Device, Creates Trust
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's closing chain in Lab 1C, credited to Jocko Willink's "discipline equals freedom": discipline gives you reliability, reliability gives you confidence, and confidence gives you "decisions you can defend" (Lab 1C transcript 00:05:48 to 00:05:54) or "decisions you can actually act on" (Lab_1c PDF p.4). The claim just before it: "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures. A procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (transcript 00:04:45–00:05:02). Weber returns to the same chain twice more in the course. In Webinar 3 he operationalizes it as three practices — document repeatable procedures, set strategic direction with explicit decision boundaries, and give staff regular direct feedback — on the stated argument that this reduces ambiguity and gives both leaders and staff more room for focused work (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–00:38). In Module 6B Part B he applies the same chain to interdisciplinary communication: "the better educated the staff are... the less translation is needed. ... That frees up time for decision-making, problem-solving, and adaptation in real time" (Module_6B_Part_B PDF p.1).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is that undocumented procedures create ambiguity, and ambiguity is what forces re-explanation, second-guessing, and disputes after the fact ("we took two measurements... which one is right?" PDF p.4). Writing the procedure down once removes the need to re-litigate it under pressure. Weber's Webinar 3 material makes the same "frees attention" claim explicitly: predictable communication and clear roles reduce the time a leader spends interpreting routine requests, freeing that attention for planning and harder problems (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 00:00–00:59, 02:52–05:05).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any point where Eric is deciding whether a documented SOP is worth the paperwork: onboarding a new staff member or intern, standardizing a force-plate or GPS procedure, or writing a credential-vault protocol. **Eric's baseline:** a secure credential-vault protocol is already named as needed but not yet implemented [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4], and the intern curriculum's stated design principle is to teach "the how" (hands-on technical training) alongside "the why" (conceptual education) [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1]. **Inference:** the how is the procedure that makes the why defensible later.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — This is a claim about where trust in a decision comes from, not a claim that more documentation is always better; Weber gives no guidance on how much procedure is enough or when documentation itself becomes the bottleneck. It also assumes the underlying test or measure is worth running at all — see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] for that prior question.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own test: "if you started a job this week as a lead in a department, would you be able to walk in and say, this is how we're going to operate?" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:05:13–00:05:23). **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's own Playbook still documents a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord collection SOP, even though roster-wide NordBord testing for football was retired after January 2023 [method-baseline.md Tensions #8]. **Inference:** this is the failure mode Weber warns against here, a procedure that fell out of sync with a decision that had already been made.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this principle closes out. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — a structure that depends on this same procedure-first discipline. 13	
14	# Decide the Means Before the Modality, and the Modality Before the Technology
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's ordering rule for any training, testing, or monitoring decision: first name the **means** (the physical quality or question you are trying to change or answer: Weber's examples are creating a stretch-shortening cycle, improving vertical stiffness, Lab 1A transcript 00:02:00 to 00:02:10; strength, stiffness, deceleration, asymmetry, rehab tolerance, Lab_1A PDF p.2), then choose the **modality** (the drill, test, or method), and only then pick the **technology**. Weber twice credits means-versus-modality to someone else, not himself: the blog states it directly, the distinction "comes from old Russian training literature" (Lab_1A PDF p.1); the transcript's "old Russian coaching accent" (00:01:53) is an ASR error. Later in the same recording he adds, "an old thing. It's not mine" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:09:37–00:09:41). The same modality can serve different means: a sprint dribble drill can teach frontside mechanics or teach vertical force application depending on the coach's intent (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:28–00:03:09). He restates the same ordering twice more across the course: in Webinar 1 Part II, the summary reports that staff should begin with the athlete question or problem and only then select a measurement tool, rather than starting from the equipment on hand (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 00:00–02:14); and in Lab 2C's written material, the operating principle is stated directly: "Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then choose the technology" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's rationale: when technology leads, "we have force plates, so we should jump" and "we have GPS, so we should report something" become the operating logic, which he calls technology-led practice that "creates noise" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). Weber's own stated point is that without this shared language, "if people don't get that context, they're going to struggle with your communication" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:52–00:03:57). **Inference:** naming the means first likely gives staff a shared reason for a drill or test, so a leader can ask "what's the mean, why are you doing it?" and get an answer staff and athletes can act on (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:42–00:04:32).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any time a new device, test, or drill is proposed because it is available rather than because a specific quality or question has been named first. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's current Applied Performance data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport or question, which Eric's own gap analysis already flags as a usability problem [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]. **Inference:** this principle gives that gap a specific fix order, name the question and quality per sport first, then map which existing technology already answers it, before adding anything new.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that the technology still has real limitations that shape what's possible ("the technology is going to have limitations, of course, but the technology may be able to be applied in different ways," Lab 1A transcript, 00:04:38–00:04:50); this is an ordering rule for decision-making, not a claim that tool constraints are irrelevant. It also does not resolve which quality matters most for a given sport or phase, only the sequence in which the question gets asked.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's CM2 athlete-stage map (see [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]]) is the means-first vocabulary he built to make this ordering usable day to day: staff say where an athlete sits (control, movement, capacity, maximum) before discussing which drill or device to use next.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]] — the shared-language framework this principle is meant to produce. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the same purpose-first ordering applied specifically to monitoring vs. testing decisions. [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the companion discipline once a measurement is in hand.
27

**What it is** — Weber's term for a specific reliability failure mode: a test keeps the same name over time while its warm-up, positioning, verbal instructions, or acceptance rules quietly change, so results are no longer comparable across sessions or staff even though the label on the report looks consistent (Podcast 1 summary, 02:19–03:03 and 04:24–05:31). **Why it works** — **Inference:** protocol drift is dangerous specifically because it is likely invisible in the data itself; a change in average or peak value looks like an athlete change unless someone knows the procedure changed underneath it. Weber's own stated companion point, per the lesson summary, is a statistical-interpretation one: know the tool's and the local process's reliability before calling any individual change meaningful, and distinguish measurement noise from a change that warrants action (Podcast 1 summary, 03:03–03:17, 05:31–06:48).

**When NOT to apply** — This principle addresses procedural consistency, not whether the test itself is the right one to run. **Inference:** a perfectly standardized bad test is still a bad test (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]]). It also does not by itself tell you the size of the error band a given procedure produces — that requires the reliability statistics in [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]].

# Discipline Equals Freedom: Procedure, Not the Device, Creates Trust

**What it is** — Weber's closing chain in Lab 1C, credited to Jocko Willink's "discipline equals freedom": discipline gives you reliability, reliability gives you confidence, and confidence gives you "decisions you can defend" (Lab 1C transcript 00:05:48 to 00:05:54) or "decisions you can actually act on" (Lab_1c PDF p.4). The claim just before it: "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures. A procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (transcript 00:04:45–00:05:02). Weber returns to the same chain twice more in the course. In Webinar 3 he operationalizes it as three practices — document repeatable procedures, set strategic direction with explicit decision boundaries, and give staff regular direct feedback — on the stated argument that this reduces ambiguity and gives both leaders and staff more room for focused work (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–00:38). In Module 6B Part B he applies the same chain to interdisciplinary communication: "the better educated the staff are... the less translation is needed. ... That frees up time for decision-making, problem-solving, and adaptation in real time" (Module_6B_Part_B PDF p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is that undocumented procedures create ambiguity, and ambiguity is what forces re-explanation, second-guessing, and disputes after the fact ("we took two measurements... which one is right?" PDF p.4). Writing the procedure down once removes the need to re-litigate it under pressure. Weber's Webinar 3 material makes the same "frees attention" claim explicitly: predictable communication and clear roles reduce the time a leader spends interpreting routine requests, freeing that attention for planning and harder problems (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 00:00–00:59, 02:52–05:05).

**When to apply** — Any point where Eric is deciding whether a documented SOP is worth the paperwork: onboarding a new staff member or intern, standardizing a force-plate or GPS procedure, or writing a credential-vault protocol. **Eric's baseline:** a secure credential-vault protocol is already named as needed but not yet implemented [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4], and the intern curriculum's stated design principle is to teach "the how" (hands-on technical training) alongside "the why" (conceptual education) [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1]. **Inference:** the how is the procedure that makes the why defensible later.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a claim about where trust in a decision comes from, not a claim that more documentation is always better; Weber gives no guidance on how much procedure is enough or when documentation itself becomes the bottleneck. It also assumes the underlying test or measure is worth running at all — see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] for that prior question.

**Example** — Weber's own test: "if you started a job this week as a lead in a department, would you be able to walk in and say, this is how we're going to operate?" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:05:13–00:05:23). **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's own Playbook still documents a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord collection SOP, even though roster-wide NordBord testing for football was retired after January 2023 [method-baseline.md Tensions #8]. **Inference:** this is the failure mode Weber warns against here, a procedure that fell out of sync with a decision that had already been made.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this principle closes out. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — a structure that depends on this same procedure-first discipline. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]] — the communication-specific application from Webinar 3.

PDF p.4). Writing the procedure down once removes the need to re-litigate it under pressure. Weber's Webinar 3 material makes the same "frees attention" claim explicitly: predictable communication and clear roles reduce the time a leader spends interpreting routine requests, freeing that attention for planning and harder problems (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 00:00–00:59, 02:52–05:05).

**When to apply** — Any point where Eric is deciding whether a documented SOP is worth the paperwork: onboarding a new staff member or intern, standardizing a force-plate or GPS procedure, or writing a credential-vault protocol. **Eric's baseline:** a secure credential-vault protocol is already named as needed but not yet implemented [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4], and the intern curriculum's stated design principle is to teach "the how" (hands-on technical training) alongside "the why" (conceptual education) [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1]. **Inference:** the how is the procedure that makes the why defensible later.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a claim about where trust in a decision comes from, not a claim that more documentation is always better; Weber gives no guidance on how much procedure is enough or when documentation itself becomes the bottleneck. It also assumes the underlying test or measure is worth running at all: see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] for that prior question.

**Example** — Weber's own test: "if you started a job this week as a lead in a department, would you be able to walk in and say, this is how we're going to operate?" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:05:13–00:05:23). **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's own Playbook still documents a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord collection SOP, even though roster-wide NordBord testing for football was retired after January 2023 [method-baseline.md Tensions #8]. **Inference:** this is the failure mode Weber warns against here, a procedure that fell out of sync with a decision that had already been made.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this principle closes out. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — a structure that depends on this same procedure-first discipline. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]] — the communication-specific application from Webinar 3.

# Decide the Means Before the Modality, and the Modality Before the Technology

**What it is** — Weber's ordering rule for any training, testing, or monitoring decision: first name the **means** (the physical quality or question you are trying to change or answer: Weber's examples are creating a stretch-shortening cycle, improving vertical stiffness, Lab 1A transcript 00:02:00 to 00:02:10; strength, stiffness, deceleration, asymmetry, rehab tolerance, Lab_1A PDF p.2), then choose the **modality** (the drill, test, or method), and only then pick the **technology**. Weber twice credits means-versus-modality to someone else, not himself: the blog states it directly, the distinction "comes from old Russian training literature" (Lab_1A PDF p.1); the transcript's "old Russian coaching accent" (00:01:53) is an ASR error. Later in the same recording he adds, "an old thing. It's not mine" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:09:37–00:09:41). The same modality can serve different means: a sprint dribble drill can teach frontside mechanics or teach vertical force application depending on the coach's intent (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:28–00:03:09). He restates the same ordering twice more across the course: in Webinar 1 Part II, the summary reports that staff should begin with the athlete question or problem and only then select a measurement tool, rather than starting from the equipment on hand (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 00:00–02:14); and in Lab 2C's written material, the operating principle is stated directly: "Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then choose the technology" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's rationale: when technology leads, "we have force plates, so we should jump" and "we have GPS, so we should report something" become the operating logic, which he calls technology-led practice that "creates noise" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). Weber's own stated point is that without this shared language, "if people don't get that context, they're going to struggle with your communication" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:52–00:03:57). **Inference:** naming the means first likely gives staff a shared reason for a drill or test, so a leader can ask "what's the mean, why are you doing it?" and get an answer staff and athletes can act on (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:42–00:04:32).

**When to apply** — Any time a new device, test, or drill is proposed because it is available rather than because a specific quality or question has been named first. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's current Applied Performance data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport or question, which Eric's own gap analysis already flags as a usability problem [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]. **Inference:** this principle gives that gap a specific fix order, name the question and quality per sport first, then map which existing technology already answers it, before adding anything new.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that the technology still has real limitations that shape what's possible ("the technology is going to have limitations, of course, but the technology may be able to be applied in different ways," Lab 1A transcript, 00:04:38–00:04:50); this is an ordering rule for decision-making, not a claim that tool constraints are irrelevant. It also does not resolve which quality matters most for a given sport or phase, only the sequence in which the question gets asked.

**Example** — Weber's CM2 athlete-stage map (see [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]]) is the means-first vocabulary he built to make this ordering usable day to day: staff say where an athlete sits (control, movement, capacity, maximum) before discussing which drill or device to use next.

**Related** — [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]] — the shared-language framework this principle is meant to produce. # Protocol Drift: A Test Can Keep Its Name While Everything Else Changes

**What it is** — Weber's term for a specific reliability failure mode: a test keeps the same name over time while its warm-up, positioning, verbal instructions, or acceptance rules quietly change, so results are no longer comparable across sessions or staff even though the label on the report looks consistent (Podcast 1 summary, 02:19–03:03 and 04:24–05:31). His fix is the same one from Lab 1C: standardize and document those details before comparing results across time or personnel (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]).

**Why it works** — **Inference:** protocol drift is dangerous specifically because it is likely invisible in the data itself; a change in average or peak value looks like an athlete change unless someone knows the procedure changed underneath it. Weber's own stated companion point, per the lesson summary, is a statistical-interpretation one: know the tool's and the local process's reliability before calling any individual change meaningful, and distinguish measurement noise from a change that warrants action (Podcast 1 summary, 03:03–03:17, 05:31–06:48).

**When to apply** — Any time staff turnover occurs on a testing team, a vendor pushes a software update that changes default settings, or a test is handed from one tester to another without a written procedure to follow. **Eric's baseline:** the current CMJ family runs a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol on ForceDecks [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], which is the kind of documented procedure this principle argues protects comparability. **Eric's baseline:** Eric's own corpus also shows two protocol documents giving different cueing instructions for the same CMJ test, the Assessment Manual says "do not coach the strategy of jumping," while Force Plate Testing V3 gives specific verbal cues [method-baseline.md Tensions #5]. **Inference:** two written protocols giving different cueing for the same test (Tension #5), one possibly legacy (Tension #4), is the documentation-side version of protocol drift: the fix is to retire or reconcile one document so staff cannot run the same-named test two ways.

**When NOT to apply** — This principle addresses procedural consistency, not whether the test itself is the right one to run. **Inference:** a perfectly standardized bad test is still a bad test (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]]). It also does not by itself tell you the size of the error band a given procedure produces — that requires the reliability statistics in [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]].

**Example** — Weber places any single product or test within a wider system: he warns against treating one red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete, and against collecting a measure without a defined question behind it (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24, 08:45–09:19). **Inference:** both are symptoms of a department that has not documented what a given result is supposed to trigger.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit that catches undocumented procedure. [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — the companion discipline against reacting to a single result. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where "what triggers action" gets formally defined.

# Measurement vs. Inference

**What it is** — Weber's distinction between what a tool actually captures (a **measurement**: force, distance, speed, displacement) and the explanation applied to that output (an **inference**: fatigue, tissue status, readiness) (Lab 2A summary, 00:00–01:45). His examples, per the lesson summary: calling a lower countermovement-jump result neurological fatigue, or a GPS change tissue stress: neither label follows directly from the measurement alone, and athletes can produce a similar output through a different movement strategy, so a stable score can hide a real change in mechanics (01:45–03:20). His stated communication rule: report what was measured, identify what is being inferred, state your confidence in that inference, and recommend the next exposure or check (05:02–06:02).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated reasons: overstating certainty "is what drives coaches crazy" (Lab_2a PDF p.2; transcript 00:02:09 to 00:02:17), and because "humans are an incredibly redundant system" the same output can hide different strategies (Lab_2a PDF p.2), so an inference has to be built by triangulation to a probability, not asserted (PDF p.3; transcript 00:03:20 to 00:04:01). **Inference:** collapsing the distinction likely lets a causal story ride along silently with a number, so the story gets treated with the same confidence as the measurement itself. Naming the inference as an inference forces an explicit confidence statement instead of an implicit one, and makes the underlying reasoning available for someone else to challenge.

**When to apply** — Any report or conversation where a device output is being used to say something about the athlete's internal state (fatigue, readiness, tissue tolerance) rather than just the output itself. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring]. **Inference:** this framework's discipline would ask the same question of mRSI that Weber asks of his CMJ example, what is actually measured (jump-derived force/time output), and what is being inferred from it (neuromuscular readiness), stated with what confidence.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication and reasoning discipline, not a claim that inference is unreliable or should be avoided; Weber's own examples (hamstring context: injury history, strength tests, jumping/hopping, speed exposure, running mechanics) show that combining several measurements to support one inference is the intended use, not a replacement for inference altogether (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02). It also does not by itself tell you whether an observed change exceeds measurement noise — see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question.

**Example** — Weber treats one test returning to baseline as one data point, not a stand-alone clearance, in his hamstring illustration (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02), the same discipline generalized into a full framework in [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]].

**Related** — [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]]: combining multiple inferences before acting on any one of them. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]: whether the measurement itself is trustworthy before it is interpreted. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]]: the upstream discipline of naming the question before choosing what to measure.

# Monitoring vs. Testing

**What it is** — Weber's separation of two questions that are often mashed together. **Monitoring** answers "has something changed right now," sits on a days-to-weeks horizon, and is "status and trend": day-to-day jump performance, session exposure/tolerance, readiness markers, short-term fatigue signals, feeding load adjustments, recovery decisions, and progression/regression calls (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1). **Testing** answers "have we improved capacity across a training phase," sits on a weeks-to-months horizon, and is "progress": pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two, evaluating whether the program is working (p.1). His explicit warning: short-term monitoring methods (rolling averages, exponentially weighted moving averages) are built to detect drift from a recent baseline, not to answer whether capacity improved across a training phase: "different questions require different analysis" (p.1–2). His communication checklist for either one: state what is being evaluated, why, how often, what output the coach will receive, and what different results would trigger, before pressure to act arrives (p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated point is that different questions require different analysis (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). **Inference:** a rolling baseline moves with the athlete, so it can hide a slow, real change in capacity even while flagging every short-term dip; conversely, comparing two widely separated phase blocks would not catch a same-week acute status change. Using the wrong analysis method for the question likely produces a plausible-looking number that answers a different question than the one being asked.

**When to apply** — Whenever a metric is being tracked at both a daily/weekly cadence and used to make phase-level claims about program effectiveness. **Eric's baseline:** the baseline states a preference for weekly tracking over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment]. **Inference:** this is a real tension worth naming: Weber's framework would say that weekly cadence is monitoring (a status/trend check), and it still needs a separate, phase-block comparison to answer the testing question of whether the athlete actually improved. The two are not substitutes for each other even when the same test (e.g., daily CMJ for mRSI) feeds both.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: single-number illustrations in the course, such as the 12% RFD change Weber dismisses as "well inside our range of variability with the MDC" (Lab 2E transcript 00:04:08 to 00:04:24), are local examples, not transferable thresholds; the lesson summary adds the same caveat (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]). This framework also does not resolve which specific quality to monitor or test for a given sport — that is the prior question in [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]].

**Example** — Weber's decision-matrix template: "if we get this result, we do these steps, owned by these people, reviewed at this time point," worked through for an eccentric-knee-flexor-force drop (confirm test quality/re-test, physio screen and ROM checks, adjust exposure plan, reassess immediately and at 24 hours, progress only when stable) (p.2).

**Related** — [[heuristic--rolling-baselines-miss-gradual-drift]]: the specific failure mode this framework warns against. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]: the formal structure for the "if this, then that" decision matrix Weber describes here. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]]: the shared "name the quality first" operating principle.

# Protocol Drift: A Test Can Keep Its Name While Everything Else Changes

**What it is** — Weber's term for a specific reliability failure mode: a test keeps the same name over time while its warm-up, positioning, verbal instructions, or acceptance rules quietly change, so results are no longer comparable across sessions or staff even though the label on the report looks consistent (Podcast 1 summary, 02:19–03:03 and 04:24–05:31). His fix is the same one from Lab 1C: standardize and document those details before comparing results across time or personnel (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]).

**Why it works** — **Inference:** protocol drift is dangerous specifically because it is likely invisible in the data itself; a change in average or peak value looks like an athlete change unless someone knows the procedure changed underneath it. Weber's own stated companion point, per the lesson summary, is a statistical-interpretation one: know the tool's and the local process's reliability before calling any individual change meaningful, and distinguish measurement noise from a change that warrants action (Podcast 1 summary, 03:03–03:17, 05:31–06:48).

**When to apply** — Any time staff turnover occurs on a testing team, a vendor pushes a software update that changes default settings, or a test is handed from one tester to another without a written procedure to follow. **Eric's baseline:** the current CMJ family runs a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol on ForceDecks [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], which is the kind of documented procedure this principle argues protects comparability. **Eric's baseline:** Eric's own corpus also shows two protocol documents giving different cueing instructions for the same CMJ test, the Assessment Manual says "do not coach the strategy of jumping," while Force Plate Testing V3 gives specific verbal cues [method-baseline.md Tensions #5]. **Inference:** two written protocols giving different cueing for the same test (Tension #5), one possibly legacy (Tension #4), is the documentation-side version of protocol drift: the fix is to retire or reconcile one document so staff cannot run the same-named test two ways.

**When NOT to apply** — This principle addresses procedural consistency, not whether the test itself is the right one to run. **Inference:** a perfectly standardized bad test is still a bad test (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]]). It also does not by itself tell you the size of the error band a given procedure produces — that requires the reliability statistics in [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]].

**Example** — Weber places any single product or test within a wider system: he warns against treating one red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete, and against collecting a measure without a defined question behind it (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24, 08:45–09:19). **Inference:** both are symptoms of a department that has not documented what a given result is supposed to trigger.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]: the audit that catches undocumented procedure. [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]]: the companion discipline against reacting to a single result. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]: where "what triggers action" gets formally defined.
